lessons.title: The spectrum and the three divisions of EW
lessons.summary: Explain what the electromagnetic spectrum is and classify an activity by its purpose.

sections.heading: Why the spectrum matters
sections.text: The electromagnetic spectrum covers the full range of electromagnetic radiation. Radios, radars, and satellite navigation all depend on portions of it. The electromagnetic operational environment describes the electromagnetic conditions and activity relevant to an operation. Those conditions can affect whether systems work as intended.

sections.heading: Classify the activity by its purpose
sections.text: Electromagnetic warfare uses electromagnetic or directed energy to control use of the spectrum or affect an adversary. Electromagnetic attack (EA) acts against adversary capability. Electromagnetic protection (EP) protects friendly people, facilities, and equipment from harmful effects of spectrum use. Electromagnetic support (ES) detects or identifies emissions to inform decisions. More than one division can contribute to the same mission.

sections.heading: Read the doctrine
sections.text: Read the JP 3-85 Executive Summary and Chapter I overview. Look up EA, EP, ES, and EW in glossary Part II.

questions.prompt: Which three divisions make up EW?
questions.answer: Electromagnetic attack, electromagnetic protection, and electromagnetic support.

questions.prompt: An exercise team identifies an unexpected emission so staff can understand the environment. Which division matches that purpose?
questions.answer: Electromagnetic support.

questions.prompt: A unit protects friendly equipment from harmful electromagnetic effects. Which division fits?
questions.answer: Electromagnetic protection.

objectives: Distinguish EMS, EMOE and EW
Identify EA, EP and ES by purpose

lessons.title: Spectrum management and interference
lessons.summary: Explain why organizations coordinate spectrum use and distinguish an observation from a cause.

sections.heading: Coordinate a shared resource
sections.text: Different users can need the same or overlapping parts of the spectrum. Spectrum management brings together planning, engineering, and administrative work so users can meet requirements under applicable rules. Frequency assignments and coordination help compatible users operate alongside each other.

sections.heading: Describe the symptom first
sections.text: Interference can arise from friendly systems, civilian activity, or other electromagnetic conditions. A brief failure during an exercise establishes a symptom. Staff can compare observations, check for conflicts, and record what remains unknown before drawing a conclusion about the cause.

sections.heading: Read the doctrine
sections.text: Read the introductory paragraphs of JP 3-85 Appendix A. Use the Army Communicator article's Collaboration Is Combat Power section to connect the concept to the Army spectrum manager role.

terms: Spectrum management — planning and coordination of spectrum use
Frequency assignment — authorized use of a frequency under specified conditions
EMI — electromagnetic interference that degrades system performance
Deconfliction — coordination to prevent incompatible activities from interfering with one another

questions.prompt: Two exercise teams request overlapping spectrum use. What staff function can assess the conflict?
questions.answer: Spectrum management.

questions.prompt: What can you conclude from an unexplained interruption alone?
questions.answer: An interruption occurred. Its cause still needs evidence.

questions.prompt: Why coordinate spectrum requirements early?
questions.answer: Early coordination gives staff time to identify conflicts and reconcile requirements before they affect other users.

objectives: Explain why spectrum use needs coordination

sections.heading: Who contributes what
sections.text: Commanders establish objectives and priorities. Staff integrate inputs from operations, intelligence, signal, and other functions into a common understanding. The spectrum manager helps reconcile spectrum requirements. EW personnel contribute expertise about electromagnetic conditions and EW capabilities relevant to the mission.

sections.heading: How the pieces fit
sections.text: Cyberspace electromagnetic activities (CEMA) provide an Army context for coordinating related work across the staff. The public Army Communicator overview describes spectrum managers collaborating with EW, cyber, intelligence, and operations staff. The ATP 3-12.4 preface identifies platoon leaders and platoon sergeants as its primary audience.

sections.heading: Read the doctrine
sections.text: Read FM 3-12 Chapter 4 for Army CEMA coordination, and the ATP 3-12.4 preface for the platoon's audience and responsibilities. The Army Communicator section Collaboration Is Combat Power connects spectrum management with staff integration. Continue with the publication courses for chapter-based study.

lessons.title: How joint forces coordinate spectrum use
lessons.summary: Explain the relationship among the joint force commander, service components, and the joint electromagnetic spectrum operations cell.

sections.heading: A shared operating environment
sections.text: A joint force's components operate in a shared electromagnetic environment. Joint electromagnetic spectrum operations (JEMSO) bring together electromagnetic warfare and spectrum management so the force can prioritize, synchronize, and deconflict activities in support of joint objectives.

sections.heading: Coordinate across components
sections.text: Service components bring their requirements and subject-matter expertise. The joint electromagnetic spectrum operations cell (JEMSOC) helps coordinate activities for the joint force commander. Its work can include aligning requirements across components and addressing conflicts with partners.

sections.heading: Read the doctrine
sections.text: Read the JP 3-85 Executive Summary and Chapter II introduction. Compare the responsibilities discussed there with the opening Purpose and Summary of Changes in CJCSM 3320.01D.

Service component — a service's organization participating in a joint force

questions.prompt: What two areas does JEMSO bring together?

questions.prompt: What does the JEMSOC help the joint force commander do?
questions.answer: Coordinate and integrate joint electromagnetic spectrum operations.

questions.prompt: Two service components have conflicting spectrum requirements in a tabletop exercise. Why surface that conflict at joint level?

sections.heading: Start with a question
sections.text: For Army-level framing, begin with FM 3-12 Chapter 1. Use JP 3-85 for the joint framework, ATP 3-12.3 for EW techniques, ATP 3-12.4 for platoon responsibilities, and ATP 6-02.70 for spectrum management. Each course identifies its verified reading edition and maps its chapters and appendices.

sections.heading: Verify the edition
sections.text: Check the publication number, title, basic edition date, and listed changes. A change sheet can carry a newer date than the cover. lessons.title: Cyberspace, the spectrum, and the operational environment
lessons.summary: Describe the relationships among cyberspace, the electromagnetic spectrum, and the Army's view of an operational environment.
objectives: Distinguish an operating domain, a dimension, and a shared spectrum resource.
Explain how cyber and spectrum dependencies can span several domains.

sections.heading: Domains and dimensions answer different questions
sections.text: FM 3-12 describes an operational environment through five domains and three dimensions. Air, land, maritime, space, and cyberspace describe areas in which forces operate. The human, physical, and information dimensions provide ways to examine conditions within those domains. A service issue, for example, can have a physical component, an information consequence, and a human decision at the same time. The classes help a staff ask different questions about one situation.

sections.heading: Cyberspace connects physical systems and data
sections.text: Cyberspace includes interconnected information technology, the data those systems hold, and supporting connections. A team may rely on a service hosted far from the place where its personnel work. An outage several steps away can interrupt a local decision process. Identify the service first and trace its dependencies. A system can be physically close to the user while the data or support behind it is remote.

sections.heading: Use of the spectrum cuts across domains
sections.text: Electromagnetic spectrum access matters to wireless communications, sensing, and timing. It also supports some cyberspace connections. A radio link can carry digitized information, for example, while sharing a physical spectrum environment with civilian and other authorized users. Examining access and dependencies together helps planners describe what may change when a service becomes unavailable.

questions.prompt: What does the information dimension help the staff examine?
questions.answer: Information and its effects on decisions and behavior within the environment.

questions.prompt: Is the electromagnetic spectrum listed as one of the five Army domains?
questions.answer: The five domains are air, land, maritime, space, and cyberspace. The spectrum is a shared physical resource used across domains.

questions.prompt: Give an example of a local function with a remote cyberspace dependency.
questions.answer: A local decision staff relies on a remotely hosted data and analysis service.

lessons.title: Threats, hazards, and confidence in attribution
lessons.summary: Classify observations, hazards, and threat hypotheses without assuming the cause of a degraded service.
objectives: Distinguish a condition or hazard from an actor with capability and intent to harm.
Explain how state, non-state, hybrid, and insider categories describe different aspects of threats.

sections.heading: Characterize exposure before attributing intent
sections.text: A hazard can harm people, equipment, or operations through conditions or events. A threat involves an actor or force with capability and intent to cause harm. Environmental effects, faults, and events caused by friendly activity can present hazards even where no hostile action is involved. A degraded service can result from any of these conditions. A staff should identify the consequence and preserve evidence while the cause is still being assessed.

sections.heading: Read actor labels as context
sections.text: The chapter discusses states, peer threats, hybrid threats, non-state actors, and insiders. Those categories help describe context, resources, access, or combinations of capabilities. For example, insider status concerns a person's connection or access to the organization. It does not independently explain the source of a given incident. Staff can use categories to shape questions about the environment while leaving individual judgments to the evidence.

sections.heading: Use evidence to update confidence
sections.text: In a classroom scenario, a test network becomes unavailable shortly after a weather event. The timing suggests a possible environmental cause. Reports about dependent services, equipment condition, and whether failures occurred elsewhere can test that hypothesis. Write down the direct observations, plausible explanations, and confidence in each interpretation. This makes the report useful even while the cause is unresolved and allows later evidence to change the assessment.

questions.prompt: What features distinguish a threat in the doctrine's definition?
questions.answer: A relevant actor or force has the capability and intent to harm.

questions.prompt: What can staff establish immediately after losing a service?
questions.answer: The observed service loss, its timing, and any known operational impact.

questions.prompt: Why preserve alternative explanations in an initial report?
questions.answer: Subsequent evidence can test the explanations and improve the confidence of the assessment.

lessons.title: Systems analysis for friendly resilience
lessons.summary: Trace dependencies in a fictional friendly service and explain how they affect resilience and risk.
objectives: Identify system components, functions, dependencies, and assumptions.
Describe a systems analysis output that supports a protection decision.

sections.heading: Start with a function people need
sections.text: A system consists of elements that interact or depend on one another. In a training scenario, consider a classroom status dashboard. Its function is to give instructors a consistent view of attendance. It depends on user accounts, a network path, an application, power, and the people who enter data. Each element matters because of its contribution to the function. Start with the output users need, then ask which elements make it possible.

sections.heading: Trace consequences across boundaries
sections.text: A change in one element can affect another. A dashboard may load while its data is stale because the collection service stopped updating it. Two services that appear independent can share an account provider or a network link. During a protection review, show known relationships and flag those that are still assumptions. Consider what functions would remain available if a shared dependency became unreliable.

sections.heading: Present the findings in decision terms
sections.text: An analysis output should make relationships and consequences easy to verify. List the function at risk, which dependencies account for that risk, the observed evidence, and any uncertainty. If instructors can continue using an independent attendance record, identify that continuity option and describe what information may be delayed. The decision-maker can then compare the consequence of an outage with the effort required to prepare or test an alternative.

questions.prompt: Why begin a systems analysis with a function?
questions.answer: It establishes what users need and makes the significance of components and dependencies clear.

questions.prompt: Two services rely on the same identity system. What is the implication?
questions.answer: A common service failure could affect both.

questions.prompt: How should a suspected dependency appear?
questions.answer: As a stated assumption or hypothesis with a way to check it.

lessons.title: Army network responsibilities and cyberspace defense
lessons.summary: Distinguish routine network operation, protective cybersecurity, and coordinated action on a specific cyber threat.
objectives: Explain the relationship between the DOD information network and its Army portion.
Identify where local defenders, service providers, and designated defense forces contribute.

sections.heading: Identify which organization owns the service
sections.text: The Department of Defense information network covers DOD information capabilities and associated processes. The Army portion supports Army information services and depends on systems and providers shared across the department. A local unit may be responsible for an endpoint or mission service while a separate provider operates an enterprise dependency. Identifying the service owner makes it easier to route support requests and coordinate decisions.

sections.heading: Protection and response run alongside operations
sections.text: Network operations keep authorized services available. Cybersecurity applies protective measures that reduce risk to networks, systems, and information. Cyberspace defense addresses specific threats against protected cyberspace and supports restoration of a secure configuration. Local defenders, cybersecurity service providers, and designated defense forces bring different responsibilities. Some incidents call for support beyond the local team even when that team first observes the problem.

sections.heading: Use the distinction in a case study
sections.text: A classroom network application may go offline during scheduled maintenance. Operations staff would check the authorized change and communicate its expected service impact. An unexpected security alert calls for coordination with the responsible cybersecurity personnel, using recorded observations and established reporting channels. The same service may be affected in each case, while the evidence, organization responsible, and immediate decision differ.

terms: DODIN — Department of Defense information network
DODIN-A — Army portion of the DOD information network

questions.prompt: What does DODIN-A refer to?
questions.answer: The Army portion of the Department of Defense information network.

questions.prompt: Why identify who operates a shared enterprise dependency?
questions.answer: So requests and incident responsibilities reach the organization with visibility and authority over it.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a specific defense incident from a scheduled outage?
questions.answer: Evidence of a security threat or policy violation calls for coordinated security analysis and response.

lessons.title: EW divisions, protection, and organizational roles
lessons.summary: Connect each division of EW to its purpose and recognize the unit and staff roles in applying it.
objectives: Distinguish electromagnetic attack, protection, and support by intent.
Explain how a unit capability and a staff coordination function complement each other.

sections.heading: Classify by the purpose
sections.text: Electromagnetic warfare uses electromagnetic or directed energy in actions concerning spectrum control or an adversary's capabilities. Electromagnetic attack acts against an adversary's ability to function. Electromagnetic protection addresses harmful effects on friendly people, facilities, or equipment. Electromagnetic support uses observations of electromagnetic energy to inform decisions. A scenario may include all three purposes. Name the principal purpose before classifying an individual activity.

sections.heading: Understand protective responsibilities
sections.text: Protection includes engineering choices, sound equipment management, and coordination across spectrum users. A compatibility issue links an engineering observation with a spectrum-management decision. When an exercise service degrades, the operator can report the impact and known conditions. Spectrum and technical staff can use that report when they consider alternative explanations or coordinate a response that keeps authorized services usable.

sections.heading: Connect the team and staff perspectives
sections.text: The manual illustrates a division electromagnetic warfare company and a brigade combat team electromagnetic warfare platoon. Such units bring trained personnel and capabilities. The appropriate staff helps integrate their contributions into the larger operation and coordinate shared constraints. When a formation asks for help, useful staff work clarifies its need, the available capacity, and the relationship between the team providing support and the formation receiving it.

questions.prompt: Which division preserves friendly use and protects friendly systems?
questions.answer: Electromagnetic protection.

questions.prompt: A team provides an observation to improve staff awareness. Which EW purpose fits?
questions.answer: Electromagnetic support.

questions.prompt: Why is staff integration needed when a unit already has EW capability?
questions.answer: It aligns the contribution with the operation and coordinates shared requirements and constraints.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic support, signals intelligence, and technical coordination
lessons.summary: Explain why overlapping observations can support different functions under separate authority.
objectives: Compare electromagnetic support and signals intelligence by purpose, tasking, and control.
Describe how technical coordination makes an observation useful across organizations.

sections.heading: Shared phenomena, different responsibilities
sections.text: Electromagnetic support and signals intelligence can observe similar electromagnetic activity with related capabilities. Electromagnetic support serves an operational commander's immediate information and planning needs. Signals intelligence is an intelligence discipline conducted under applicable intelligence requirements and authorities. An activity's purpose, tasking, and controlling authority determine how staff should treat it. These distinctions matter when gathering, handling, and sharing the resulting information.

sections.heading: Coordinate through the appropriate staff
sections.text: The cyber electromagnetic warfare officer and CEMA section coordinate with the intelligence staff to synchronize EW and signals intelligence. Start with the question each organization is trying to answer and identify the kinds of information each is authorized to use. Coordination can reduce redundant work and help the staff assess complementary observations. Technical control also helps assign responsibility for standards, technical direction, and consistent handling of information.

sections.heading: Keep provenance with any assessment
sections.text: In a study exercise, two organizations may receive descriptions of the same synthetic observation. Comparing them can reveal a common original source and prevent the staff from treating repeated reporting as independent confirmation. Document the source, time, intended use, and confidence, then share according to the relevant authority. If an observed environmental change is validated, it may also become an input to the formal reprogramming process.

questions.prompt: What determines whether a proposed observation activity falls under ES or SIGINT?
questions.answer: Its purpose, tasking, controlling organization, and applicable authorities.

questions.prompt: Which staff relationship supports coordination between EW and signals intelligence?
questions.answer: CEMA and the cyber electromagnetic warfare officer coordinate with the intelligence staff.

questions.prompt: Why preserve the original source of each report?
questions.answer: To understand provenance, identify duplicates, and judge how independently the evidence supports an assessment.

lessons.title: CEMA roles across echelons and the operations process
lessons.summary: Track how CEMA inputs reach command decisions and describe why its staff work changes by echelon.
objectives: Distinguish a CEMA section, a working group, and the commander.
Follow an EW or cybersecurity dependency from planning through assessment.

sections.heading: A staff function connects several specialties
sections.text: Army staffs use CEMA to integrate cyberspace and EW with the larger operation. A CEMA section includes specialists who contribute cyberspace, EW, and spectrum-management expertise. The working group provides a forum for other staff and supporting organizations to coordinate decisions and products. The commander establishes objectives and direction, and the staff translates specialized information into decisions relevant to those objectives.

sections.heading: Explain the difference an echelon makes
sections.text: A brigade's staff needs information specific to its tasks and current support relationships. A division or corps can consider resource demands and effects across several subordinate formations. Reporting should retain detail needed by the receiving organization, including the confidence and limits of the estimate. A recurring dependency can be a local readiness issue for one echelon and a cross-formation coordination problem for another.

sections.heading: Revisit the same dependency over time
sections.text: During planning, the staff identifies a required service and its constraints. Preparation confirms that users and providers understand the handoff. During execution, current operations personnel track what changed and when a decision is needed. Assessment asks whether the arrangement actually supported the mission. In a classroom exercise, these stages might track one reporting channel from assigned capacity through observed delays and a revised schedule.

questions.prompt: What is the function of a CEMA working group?
questions.answer: It brings relevant staff and organizations together to coordinate activities and products.

questions.prompt: Why may division staff ask for additional context on a brigade service issue?
questions.answer: Division may need to assess impact across formations and establish shared priorities.

questions.prompt: Which operations-process activity studies whether the intended result occurred?
questions.answer: Assessment.

lessons.title: Army CEMA and joint coordination
lessons.summary: Trace the conceptual Army-to-joint coordination relationships for cyberspace, EW, and spectrum management.
objectives: Identify why joint cyber, spectrum operations, and frequency management use different coordination channels.
Explain what an Army component headquarters contributes to the joint force.

sections.heading: Start with the problem the staff is coordinating
sections.text: An Army formation may need help resolving spectrum use, protecting a shared network, or aligning an EW contribution with a joint operation. These needs involve different expertise and authorities. The doctrine describes connections through the combatant command joint cyber center for cyberspace operations and the joint electromagnetic spectrum operations cell for EW. Spectrum management uses the joint frequency management office where that function is organized separately.

sections.heading: Integrating processes connect the staff's work
sections.text: Intelligence preparation develops the staff's understanding of the environment. Information collection helps resolve specific information needs. Targeting is a separate staff process with command oversight. Risk management evaluates hazards and controls, while knowledge management gets information to the people who need it. A loss of service can inform several of these processes, with CEMA contributing evidence about the shared dependency.

sections.heading: Relate the Army echelon to the joint force
sections.text: The Army component headquarters represents Army requirements within the joint context. Its CEMA staff helps bridge Army and joint coordination. A subordinate unit supplies timely, contextual detail about its need. The Army headquarters connects that need to wider priorities and the relevant joint function. That relationship helps explain why a locally feasible proposal may require decisions or synchronization at another level.

sections.heading: Make handoffs readable across staffs
sections.text: A joint-facing request or update should explain the friendly service, dependency, or support need in terms that another component can understand. In a simulation, two services may rely on overlapping shared resources. The deploying Army formation can describe its requirement, while joint coordination can see the commitments made by other components. Recording the resulting responsibility and decision helps ensure that the agreement travels back to the people who need it.

terms: JEMSOC — joint electromagnetic spectrum operations cell

questions.prompt: Which joint function integrates electromagnetic spectrum operations?
questions.answer: The joint electromagnetic spectrum operations cell.

questions.prompt: Why may a spectrum constraint need joint visibility?
questions.answer: Other components can use the same shared spectrum resources.

questions.prompt: What does the Army component headquarters contribute?
questions.answer: It connects Army requirements and staff coordination with the appropriate joint functions.

lessons.title: Combined arms and the competition continuum
lessons.summary: Explain how Army cyber and EW contributions change with context and work alongside joint capabilities.
objectives: Describe convergence as coordinated contributions across domains toward an objective.
Identify defensive and coordination needs that persist across competition, crisis, and armed conflict.

sections.heading: Combined arms relies on complementary contributions
sections.text: A combined arms approach relates different capabilities to the same commander's objectives. Convergence coordinates contributions across domains and echelons so their effects support one another. In the defensive context, Army staff may connect network security, continuity of communications, and spectrum compatibility to preserve joint command and control. Each function provides a different contribution. Their timing and shared dependencies determine how well they work together.

sections.heading: Context changes the emphasis
sections.text: The chapter discusses competition, crisis, and armed conflict. Staff may weigh readiness, partnerships, and longer-term coordination more heavily during competition. A crisis increases the need to confirm roles, authorities, and shared situational understanding as conditions change. In armed conflict, units may need to sustain more activity while the environment changes rapidly. The requirements for oversight, continuity, and defensive cyberspace work persist across the continuum.

sections.heading: Preserve a shared picture of what matters
sections.text: Consider a simulated joint exercise that expands during a fictional crisis. Several components need a shared communications service. A spectrum team can identify conflicts in the service's operating environment, while network defenders track its security and availability. The staff can compare both accounts and explain the impact on decisions. Making known limits and reporting responsibilities explicit gives joint partners a common basis for coordinating support.

questions.prompt: What does convergence add to a list of available capabilities?
questions.answer: Coordination across capabilities, domains, and echelons toward a common objective.

questions.prompt: Which kind of cyberspace activity remains necessary throughout the competition continuum?
questions.answer: Defensive work that preserves friendly services, capabilities, and data.

questions.prompt: Why reassess coordination in a crisis scenario?
questions.answer: Needs, responsibilities, availability, and applicable authorities can change quickly.

lessons.title: Incident response from initial event to recovery
lessons.summary: Walk through the decision points of a defensive cyber incident response using a fictional service alert.
objectives: Distinguish an observable event, a validated incident, and an assessed mission impact.
Explain the purpose of escalation, recovery confirmation, and post-incident review.

sections.heading: Classify after evaluating evidence
sections.text: An event is an observable occurrence. Some events warrant reporting or investigation, and analysis determines whether they meet incident criteria. A training network may report an unexpected login while a service continues operating. A defender preserves the relevant observations and checks whether they indicate a security violation. Separately, the service owner can explain who depends on the service and what would change if it became unreliable.

sections.heading: Keep a common timeline and assess the impact
sections.text: An initial report may be incomplete and still useful. Record when the observation occurred, which service is involved, who reported it, and what is known about impact. The appropriate team evaluates severity and coordinates response through established reporting channels. As investigators learn more, they update details and decisions in the record. Shared terminology helps units and higher organizations understand why the incident requires particular attention.

sections.heading: Establish a defensible recovery record
sections.text: Response and recovery aim to restore trusted service and understand what happened. Recovery assessment can consider whether authorized users can use the service and whether security staff have evidence that protective controls are functioning. Post-incident review uses the timeline to examine how teams detected, classified, communicated, and responded to the issue. It can reveal process or monitoring changes that matter for future incidents.

questions.prompt: Is an unusual login automatically a confirmed incident?
questions.answer: It is an event that may require analysis under applicable incident criteria.

questions.prompt: Who helps explain the operational effect of losing a service?
questions.answer: The service owner and its users, working with incident-response staff.

questions.prompt: Why preserve a timeline through recovery?
questions.answer: It supports reporting, reconstruction of decisions, and post-incident learning.

lessons.title: Running estimates, decisions, and working groups
lessons.summary: Use a running estimate to capture facts, assumptions, and recommendations and identify how staff coordinate across working groups.
objectives: Distinguish an estimate, a working group's contribution, and a published plan or order.
Explain how changes in facts or assumptions should reach the appropriate decision-maker.

sections.heading: The estimate stays live
sections.text: A running estimate captures the staff's current understanding of the situation, including facts, assumptions, status, and recommendations. A CEMA estimate considers whether requirements can be supported now and whether future plans remain feasible. A staff can update an assumption about service availability as it receives records from the responsible organization. Keep the original assumption visible where it affected an earlier decision, and record what evidence changed the judgment.

sections.heading: Separate staff products from approved direction
sections.text: The estimate and the intelligence preparation of the operational environment contribute to planning. Working groups coordinate contributions and make recommendations within their purpose. A published plan or order communicates approved direction through the command structure. They serve different readers and time horizons. When a working group identifies a problem, the relevant estimate and staff products should reflect it so that leaders can examine the effect at an appropriate decision point.

sections.heading: Bring the right question to each group
sections.text: An information collection group helps align approved information needs and collection. A protection group considers hazards and controls for friendly systems. An assessment group reviews evidence of progress and outcomes. In a classroom example, an unexplained service issue may need an observation request, a protection review, and a later assessment of recovery. Consistent terminology and shared evidence help these groups coordinate without each recreating the entire analysis.

terms: IPOE — intelligence preparation of the operational environment

questions.prompt: When does a running estimate need an update?
questions.answer: When relevant facts, assumptions, status, or recommendations change.

questions.prompt: Which product communicates the approved plan to subordinate elements?
questions.answer: The operation plan or order.

questions.prompt: Which staff forum helps evaluate whether the desired condition changed?
questions.answer: An assessment working group.

lessons.title: Support requests, approval, and authority
lessons.summary: Explain how a support request turns a capability gap into a decision for the responsible headquarters.
objectives: Distinguish a request, command approval, and applicable authority.
Explain what the requesting organization and the prospective provider contribute to the decision.
Explain why approval to forward a request and confirmation of support need separate statuses.

sections.heading: A request begins with a gap
sections.text: Army units may request external support when a requirement exceeds local capabilities or depends on another organization's role. The appendix discusses external electromagnetic warfare support and different kinds of cyberspace support. In a fictional network-defense exercise, a local administrator can see a service failure while the enterprise defender has wider visibility and responsibility. The local staff can explain the operational impact, the help it needs, and the observations that support that request.

sections.heading: Approval answers a specific question
sections.text: A commander may approve forwarding a request for support. The receiving organization validates the requirement, evaluates its responsibilities, and considers whether it can provide support. Applicable law, policy, and command direction determine who has authority to carry out an activity and under which conditions. Each judgment serves a distinct purpose. A record that says who approved what helps staff distinguish sponsorship, support availability, and authority.

sections.heading: Close the loop with the requesting staff
sections.text: The request has value only if the unit can act on the answer. A pending request leaves the planned support unresolved. A response should make the responsible organization, approved purpose, and remaining constraints clear. In an exercise, the local staff can plan for known capacity while tracking the external decision and updating the estimate when it receives confirmation.

sections.heading: A forwarded request can still have dependencies
sections.text: The examples in Appendix C distinguish the requesting unit’s decision to ask for support from what happens at a coordinating headquarters or service provider. Validation can establish that a need is understood and suitable for further consideration. It does not reserve resources or settle the authority for a requested action. If a planning estimate depends on outside assistance, list the local need, who must confirm the provider decision, and what remains uncertain. That lets the staff communicate risk while the request is being reviewed.

questions.prompt: Why would a unit seek external support?
questions.answer: Its requirement may exceed local capability or depend on an organization with a different responsibility.

questions.prompt: The unit commander approved forwarding a request. What should the staff still verify?
questions.answer: The provider's decision, availability, and the authority that applies to the activity.

questions.prompt: What should a support decision communicate back to the unit?
questions.answer: Who is responsible, what support was approved, and which conditions remain.

questions.prompt: A classroom support request is validated and forwarded, and the draft plan marks the supporting service as guaranteed. What should the plan say?
questions.answer: The request was validated and forwarded. Availability and any applicable authorization are still unconfirmed. Record that dependence as an assumption or contingency until the responsible organization confirms the support and its conditions.

lessons.title: Symptoms, attribution, and reporting
lessons.summary: Describe degraded friendly services in a way that supports investigation across spectrum and cybersecurity teams.
objectives: Distinguish observed symptoms, supporting evidence, and attribution.
Explain how local and higher-level reporting add different kinds of visibility.

sections.heading: A symptom is shared evidence
sections.text: A degraded service may prompt spectrum staff, equipment maintainers, and network defenders to review the same event. Each team sees part of the picture. In a training exercise, users might report delayed messages while a receiver remains responsive. That combination establishes an impact and narrows the questions to investigate. Several causes are still possible, including local faults, ordinary interference, service dependencies, or malicious activity.

sections.heading: Scope and timing help test explanations
sections.text: Record what service was affected, when the symptom began, and which users reported it. A second team's report can help determine whether the problem was local or shared. Confirm that independent reports came from distinct observations and use compatible time references. Staff can then distinguish a supported judgment about scope from a more tentative judgment about cause. This distinction reduces the chance that an early label will dominate a later investigation.

sections.heading: Report through the role that can investigate
sections.text: The appendix describes joint spectrum interference resolution as a reporting and coordination function. Cybersecurity staff handle suspected malicious activity on friendly networks through established incident processes. Some events require the two perspectives because a network service and a radio-dependent link can fail together. An updated report can preserve the original observation, state the current impact, and explain what remains uncertain.

questions.prompt: Two groups forward the same original message. Does that establish two independent observations?
questions.answer: It establishes one observation reported by two groups.

questions.prompt: Which details establish the scope of a service problem?
questions.answer: The affected service, timing, impacted users, and independently confirmed observations.

questions.prompt: When might spectrum and cybersecurity teams both need visibility?
questions.answer: When symptoms could involve either part of a shared service dependency or both.

lessons.sourceLocator: Appendix D, Section II, paras. D-41 to D-44 and D-51

lessons.title: Message formats as shared records
lessons.summary: Explain how standard message categories preserve meaning as reports move between teams.
objectives: Distinguish observation reports, coordination records, and change-status messages.
Identify which confirmation supports an update from requested to implemented.
Reconcile conflicting change-status records by matching the version, reporting organization, scope, and unresolved issues.

sections.heading: A standard record means the same thing to each team
sections.text: Appendix E provides EW messages and reprogramming messages. Standard formats establish what the sender and recipient expect a record to communicate. A coordination message helps recipients act together on an established decision. An observation report preserves facts that analysts or maintainers can assess. A summary consolidates work for later review. Choose among these purposes by asking what the receiving team needs to know or do.

sections.heading: A change has several distinct states
sections.text: The appendix connects reprogramming messages with requirement, response, development, and implementation phases. A record can describe a requested change, an assessed impact, or a change applied by a unit. Those states have different evidentiary value. In a classroom configuration exercise, approval to update an interpretation rule supports planned work, while an implementation record and a verification result support a claim that the work happened.

sections.heading: Keep context intact through a handoff
sections.text: When information crosses staff and organizational boundaries, its meaning depends on source, status, and time. A new report may revise an earlier observation. A later record should make the relationship clear so the recipient knows what changed and which information still applies. Confirmation by the receiving team also helps the sender distinguish successful communication from an unanswered message.

sections.heading: When the records disagree
sections.text: FM 3-12 separates a formal change request, an impact message announcing an available update, and the unit’s report of implementation. An announcement can describe who should receive an update and when it is available. It cannot establish that a particular team applied it. The unit report can establish what that team says it completed and which anomalies it observed. A follow-up verification record answers a further question about whether the changed process performs as expected.

sections.heading: Record the smallest status the evidence supports
sections.text: A classroom exercise publishes a revised classification guide. Team A confirms applying revision 2 and reports that one example still displays the old label. Team B acknowledges receiving the bulletin. The coordinator can record that revision 2 is available, that Team A reports applying it with an unresolved issue, and that Team B’s implementation is unconfirmed. A general ‘complete’ entry would erase both the reporting scope and the exception. Keep the version, team, and affected example visible so a later check can resolve the discrepancy.

questions.prompt: Which type of record preserves facts for later review?
questions.answer: An observation report or a summary, depending on whether it captures the event or consolidates several activities.

questions.prompt: What would distinguish implementation of a change from verification that it works?
questions.answer: A unit implementation report records that the change was applied and can describe anomalies. A separate check of the resulting behavior supports a claim that the change works as expected.

questions.prompt: Why identify which earlier record a new message updates?
questions.answer: It helps recipients understand what changed and which earlier details still apply.

questions.prompt: A bulletin announces revision 2 for two exercise teams. Team A reports applying it but flags a remaining error. Team B confirms receipt only. What can the coordinator mark as complete, and what needs follow-up?
questions.answer: Record that Team A reports applying revision 2, with the error still open. Team B’s receipt establishes delivery of the notice. Its implementation is unconfirmed, so obtain a team-specific update and verify the reported error before treating the rollout as resolved.

Home-station training applies those skills within a unit's mission-essential tasks and develops individual and collective proficiency. Combat training center events provide a broader environment for evaluating combined performance. Experience in one venue can inform work in the others as leaders identify which skills require practice and which problems require coordination across staff or unit boundaries.

sections.heading: Train a measurable task in context
sections.text: A useful training objective names a task, the conditions under which it occurs, and an observable standard. For example, a training staff could require teams to submit an interference observation during a fictional service interruption and preserve its time, scope, and stated confidence. Practicing several shifts can show whether the record stays useful after responsibility passes to another team. That tests a collective handoff as well as individual reporting.

sections.heading: Review results and carry them forward
sections.text: The commander owns the training program, and noncommissioned officers train individuals, crews, and small teams. The CEWO helps align relevant home-station training with mission-essential tasks and training center evaluations. After an event, compare observed performance with the standard and identify why a gap occurred. Follow-up training can then focus on the specific handoff, vocabulary, or judgment that led to the gap.

questions.prompt: Which venue ties ongoing training to the unit's essential tasks?
questions.answer: Home-station training.

questions.prompt: What makes a training standard observable?
questions.answer: It states a result or behavior that an evaluator can check.

questions.prompt: Why use a scenario spanning multiple shifts?
questions.answer: It tests whether individual reports support a collective handoff and continuing staff awareness.

lessons.title: Network hardening as risk reduction

sections.heading: Four areas protect different parts of the network
sections.text: The appendix organizes hardening around domain management, network-device management, traffic monitoring and alerts, and endpoint security. Domain management covers administrative structures and access. Device management concerns equipment configuration and upkeep. Monitoring provides evidence about what the network is doing. Endpoint security concerns the hosts and servers that users and services depend on. An organization can use these categories to identify which controls and responsibilities it should review.

sections.heading: Introduce changes with known outcomes
sections.text: A new access policy can improve security and also interrupt an authorized workflow if deployed without understanding dependencies. Test representative conditions, record the intended change, and use the appropriate change authority. In a fictional training environment, the organization can confirm that permitted users complete their normal tasks and that restricted actions require the correct privilege. Planning recovery before rollout makes failures easier to manage.

sections.heading: Keep evidence that controls work
sections.text: Configurations, alerts, patch records, and service-health observations provide different views of cybersecurity. Staff need a way to evaluate whether those records are useful and whether someone reviews and acts on them. One dashboard might show that a host stopped reporting, while a support team can explain whether it was intentionally retired or lost visibility. A hardening review brings that evidence together and records what still needs verification.

questions.prompt: Which area explains how the staff would see unusual network or device activity?
questions.answer: Traffic monitoring and alerts.

questions.prompt: Why test a new access policy with representative authorized users?
questions.answer: To verify the protective change while checking that required work remains possible.

questions.prompt: Which records help show whether endpoint maintenance is current?
questions.answer: Patch, configuration, and service-health records.

lessons.title: Army integrated reprogramming as a governed change cycle
lessons.summary: Explain why FM 3-12 treats reprogramming as a validated and governed process and distinguish the future-state model from current availability.
objectives: Describe how validated observations become requirements for change.
Explain why responsibility, approval, and result verification matter in a reprogramming cycle.

sections.heading: Change starts with validated evidence
sections.text: EW reprogramming addresses validated changes in the electromagnetic environment, relevant equipment, or practices. A report suggests that something may have changed. Technical assessment checks whether the observation is consistent and relevant. A useful requirement explains the operational consequence and why the current capability needs review. This sequence helps prioritize evidence-supported changes when several organizations submit overlapping requests or compete for limited development capacity.

sections.heading: Read the diagram as a governance model
sections.text: Appendix I describes a future-state Army integrated reprogramming cycle. It connects identifying a requirement, deciding how to respond, developing a change, and implementing it through a governed process. The governance body coordinates priorities, assigns responsibility, and approves release. Distinguish what the manual proposes for the future from the organizations, timelines, and capabilities confirmed for a particular unit.

sections.heading: Track the result after release
sections.text: A change becomes meaningful when the responsible teams can establish what was approved, what was applied, and whether it addressed the original need. In a classroom maintenance scenario, a new interpretation rule can be versioned and checked against a known set of test observations. The teams should preserve the rationale and report unexpected results. That record supports review and future decisions about the same requirement.

questions.prompt: What turns a field observation into a defensible change requirement?
questions.answer: Validation and a documented explanation of its operational relevance.

questions.prompt: Which responsibility belongs with governance in the future-state model?

questions.prompt: What should a reader infer about implementation from a future-state diagram?
questions.answer: It describes the intended model. Current deployment and availability need their own evidence.

lessons.title: Congestion, interference, and EW divisions
lessons.summary: Explain why the electromagnetic environment can be crowded and contested at the same time.
objectives: Distinguish congestion, contention, and interference.
Classify electromagnetic activities by their principal purpose.

sections.heading: A shared operating environment
sections.text: A radio, a navigation receiver, and a radar use the same physical spectrum for different purposes. Across the operational environment, military, civilian, and commercial users can all make demands on it. Congestion describes concentrated use and overlapping demand. A contested environment includes deliberate efforts by another actor to limit friendly use. The conditions can coexist, and demand may change as forces or civilian systems move or when operating hours change.

sections.heading: Start with the observed impact
sections.text: Interference describes a disturbance that degrades a system. During a laboratory exercise, a communication service might become unreliable at the same time a second device is powered on. The first observation is a change in reliability and its timing. The cause remains a hypothesis, since equipment faults and changes in the surrounding environment can produce similar symptoms. Reporting the service affected and the known conditions gives the responsible staff enough context to compare observations.

sections.heading: Classify activities by intent
sections.text: Electromagnetic support uses observations of electromagnetic energy to build awareness and inform decisions. Electromagnetic protection preserves friendly access and system performance. Electromagnetic attack is the division directed at affecting an adversary's capability. Analysts and planners may discuss all three in one mission brief because they address different needs in the same environment. Classify each activity by the job it is meant to do, even when several activities involve the same piece of equipment.

questions.prompt: An exercise area has several authorized users competing for access. What condition does this describe?
questions.answer: Congestion.

questions.prompt: An unexpected transmission is documented to inform staff awareness. Which division fits that purpose?
questions.answer: Electromagnetic support.

questions.prompt: A service interruption coincides with a second device powering on. What is established?
questions.answer: The time relationship and the impact on the service. The cause still needs evidence.

lessons.title: Staff roles and the limits of authority
lessons.summary: Identify the staff roles that integrate EW and explain why capability and permission are separate decisions.
objectives: Connect EW expertise, spectrum management, and the operations staff.
Identify when a question of authority belongs with the appropriate command and legal channels.
Distinguish a service capability description from a supported organization’s access or authority.

sections.heading: Distinct kinds of expertise
sections.text: At theater army through brigade, the CEMA section brings together EW, cyberspace, and spectrum-management expertise. The cyber electromagnetic warfare officer coordinates EW input for the staff. EW technicians and noncommissioned officers provide technical judgment and practical knowledge of EW capabilities. The spectrum manager coordinates use by many spectrum-dependent systems across the force. The section works with the operations staff to make those inputs usable in the commander's plan.

sections.heading: Echelon and staff coordination
sections.text: The staff at one echelon may identify a problem or resource need that another echelon is equipped to address. A lower echelon can explain the service affected and its immediate operational consequence, while a higher echelon can consider the needs of several subordinate formations. A clear handoff gives each level enough information to do its part. It also identifies the organization responsible for the next decision.

sections.heading: Authority and accountability
sections.text: A qualified EW team may have the personnel and means to carry out an activity. A delegation identifies which organization can exercise specified authority and the conditions that apply. The authority to conduct that activity depends on applicable law, policy, rules of engagement, and command direction. When a proposal intersects another function, such as signals intelligence, the staff involves the relevant functional and legal authorities. Recording both the decision and its conditions keeps the approval understandable when the situation or staff changes.

sections.heading: Separate capability, access, and authority
sections.text: Appendix C groups capability examples by Service. Use the headings to identify the Service context and read each entry as a description from that edition. If a reference lists a Service capability, it supports a statement about what that capability was described as doing. Availability for a particular request depends on the organization providing support and the resources it can commit. Authority for its use is a separate command question. A planning note can mark an example as a potential contribution while keeping availability and authorization open.

questions.prompt: Which role helps coordinate competing uses of a common electromagnetic resource?
questions.answer: The spectrum manager, working with the CEMA section and other staff functions.

questions.prompt: A unit has suitable equipment and trained personnel. What question still needs an answer?
questions.answer: Which authority approves the specific activity and under what conditions.

questions.prompt: What should a lower echelon convey when asking a higher one to address interference?
questions.answer: The observed impact, mission consequence, and the decision or support needed.

questions.prompt: A dated reference lists a capability under another Service. A planning note treats it as already available and approved. Which claims does the reference support, and which require other evidence?
questions.answer: It supports the edition-specific capability description and Service context. Confirm availability with the supporting organization and any applicable approval with the responsible authority before treating either as established.

lessons.title: EW inputs to planning and preparation

sections.heading: A running estimate supports choices
sections.text: The EW planner participates throughout the military decision-making process. Early questions concern mission requirements, known constraints, and assumptions. As the staff develops courses of action, the estimate records which facts affect feasibility and what uncertainties require attention. The estimate remains current after orders are issued. A changing assumption about the reliability of a shared service can affect several staff functions and may require the commander to revisit an earlier decision.

sections.heading: Organize contributions around a common problem
sections.text: The operations staff connects EW to the larger plan and distributes approved orders. The intelligence staff helps characterize the environment and the reliability of reports. The signal staff explains communications dependencies, and spectrum managers identify resource conflicts. A useful CEMA contribution states clearly what a new piece of information changes. For example, knowing that two plans depend on the same support can prompt a staff discussion of priority and timing.

sections.heading: Confirm readiness during preparation
sections.text: Preparation gives leaders a chance to examine whether the support relationships and information handoffs in the plan work in practice. Supporting teams confirm who receives reports, when conditions require escalation, and what constraints apply. Coordination between EW and signals-intelligence personnel clarifies each activity's purpose, control, and applicable authorities. Findings from a rehearsal or coordination meeting can update the running estimate before execution begins.

questions.prompt: Which product keeps EW facts and assumptions current as the plan evolves?
questions.answer: The EW running estimate.

questions.prompt: Two candidate plans depend on the same limited support. What would a useful staff contribution explain?
questions.answer: The shared dependency and how it affects feasibility, priority, and timing.

questions.prompt: Why coordinate with signals intelligence during preparation?
questions.answer: To align shared support while clarifying purpose, control, and authority for each activity.

lessons.title: Performance, effectiveness, and evidence
lessons.summary: Use measures of performance and effectiveness to interpret the results of a classroom EW readiness scenario.
objectives: Distinguish evidence that a task occurred from evidence of a changed condition.
Construct an assessment question with a baseline and a data owner.

sections.heading: Ask two different questions
sections.text: A measure of performance tracks whether an assigned task was completed to the required standard. A measure of effectiveness tracks whether an intended condition changed. For a classroom exercise on interference reporting, submitting each report before the deadline is a performance measure. Reducing the time needed by staff to identify which services have been affected is an effectiveness measure. Both can be measured, and they can produce different results in the same exercise.

sections.heading: Interpret results in context
sections.text: Imagine that all exercise teams submit their reports on schedule, but the staff still takes a long time to understand the problem. Timeliness improved and the decision process still struggled. Investigators might look at whether the reports recorded different time references or used inconsistent descriptions of the affected service. The assessment should also consider whether workload changed, which could alter how quickly the staff processes reports.

sections.heading: Build the assessment into the plan
sections.text: Decide beforehand what evidence is needed, who can collect it, and what it will be compared with. A baseline could be the response time in a previous exercise with a comparable workload. During execution, keep observations and interpretation separate. A CEWO can use that evidence to update the running estimate and describe whether the result warrants adjustment, another observation, or a different measure.

questions.prompt: A team filed its assigned reports on time. Which kind of measure does that satisfy?
questions.answer: A measure of performance.

questions.prompt: Staff identified affected services faster across comparable exercise rounds. Which kind of measure does that support?
questions.answer: A measure of effectiveness.

questions.prompt: Why name a data owner during planning?
questions.answer: So someone is accountable for collecting comparable, timely evidence for assessment.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic attack purposes and limits
lessons.summary: Classify electromagnetic attack at the level of purpose and authority and explain how its limits affect staff judgment.
objectives: Distinguish offensive and defensive electromagnetic attack from electromagnetic protection.
Explain the relevance of authorization, uncertainty, and impacts on other spectrum users.

sections.heading: Classify the activity by who or what it affects
sections.text: Electromagnetic attack is the EW division concerned with affecting an adversary's capability. The chapter distinguishes offensive and defensive uses. A defensive use may protect friendly forces by acting on a threat capability. Electromagnetic protection instead concerns the ability of friendly people, equipment, and services to withstand harmful electromagnetic effects. In a classroom classification exercise, ask where the action is directed and what outcome it is intended to produce.

sections.heading: Broad categories describe different intended effects
sections.text: The chapter discusses electromagnetic countermeasures and deception. At a conceptual level, countermeasures seek to reduce the usefulness of a spectrum-dependent capability. Electromagnetic deception concerns the information an adversary derives from electromagnetic activity. These categories describe the intent of an action. To assess whether an effect occurred, staff need evidence about the affected condition, its duration, and which interpretation the available observations support.

sections.heading: Authority and shared use shape the limits
sections.text: Electromagnetic activities may affect other users of the same environment, including friendly or civilian services. Availability of a capability is one consideration. Applicable authorities, oversight, and coordination are separate requirements. Staff can explain the intended outcome, relevant constraints, and what reliable evidence would support any later assessment. That framing links technical judgment to the accountable command decision while recognizing uncertainty about actual results.

questions.prompt: Why can a protective purpose still involve defensive electromagnetic attack?
questions.answer: The action is directed at a threat capability, with protection of friendly forces as its purpose.

questions.prompt: What separates a stated intended effect from an assessed effect?
questions.answer: An assessed effect requires supporting evidence of a changed condition.

questions.prompt: Why discuss other spectrum users during staff review?
questions.answer: An effect can also influence friendly or civilian services that rely on the shared environment.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic protection and interference reports
lessons.summary: Explain the purpose of electromagnetic protection and write a clear observation of interference for an exercise scenario.
objectives: Separate system performance observations from proposed causes.
Explain why compatibility and coordination are part of protection.

sections.heading: Protection as a design and staff responsibility
sections.text: Electromagnetic protection keeps friendly people, equipment, and functions usable in the presence of harmful electromagnetic effects. It begins with knowing which services depend on the spectrum and which other users share it. An engineering choice can improve equipment compatibility, while a staff coordination decision can resolve conflicting requirements. These activities contribute to the same protective purpose at different points in the system.

sections.heading: An interference observation earns its conclusion
sections.text: Start a classroom report with the problem the operator directly observed. State when it started, how long it persisted, what service was affected, and whether another observation independently confirmed it. An ambiguous symptom such as audio loss can have more than one cause. A staff review can compare the symptoms against equipment status and reports from other users, then record which explanations remain plausible.

sections.heading: Track whether service recovered
sections.text: A report needs to be usable by the people who maintain or coordinate the affected service. If conditions change, update the duration, affected users, and any difference between the observed impact and earlier estimates. Teams should be able to tell whether the service actually recovered or whether reporting stopped. Lessons learned can inform future planning and help explain why one coordination decision was more effective than another.

questions.prompt: A display indicates service loss. What evidence should the report start with?
questions.answer: The affected service, time, duration, and observed symptoms.

questions.prompt: Why does compatibility belong in protection planning?
questions.answer: Compatible systems are less likely to impair one another, which preserves friendly service.

questions.prompt: A second user reports the same symptom a minute later. What should the reviewer check before treating the report as independent evidence?
questions.answer: Check whether the second user made a separate observation and record what service and conditions it covers. A separately observed symptom can help establish scope and timing. A forwarded report repeats the first observation. Neither identifies the cause on its own.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic support as evidence for decisions
lessons.summary: Assess the reliability of an electromagnetic support observation and explain how it contributes to staff understanding.
objectives: Describe the purpose and tasking context of electromagnetic support.
Distinguish the source observation, analyst inference, and assessed confidence.

sections.heading: What the function contributes
sections.text: Electromagnetic support responds to an operational commander's information needs by observing electromagnetic activity. It contributes situational understanding, immediate awareness, and input to future planning. In a classroom example, a team might record that a synthetic signal appeared during a communications test. A report connects that observation to the question the staff is trying to answer so a decision-maker can judge its relevance.

sections.heading: Account for uncertainty
sections.text: Receivers observe effects at a particular time and place. Terrain, structures, weather-related propagation changes, and limitations of a measurement can change what the receiver sees. Independent observations are valuable when their context differs enough to test an explanation. Several reports copied from the same original observation have a common source, even when delivered through separate channels. Good reporting makes that relationship clear.

sections.heading: Keep interpretation traceable
sections.text: A useful report gives the time of the observation, provenance, and description of the signal, then separates any judgment about what it represents. Confidence reflects the quality and agreement of the evidence. A gap in observations can be caused by a gap in coverage, so absence of a report provides different evidence from a positive observation. Staff can revisit the judgment when new records arrive without losing track of what was known earlier.

questions.prompt: What should an analyst preserve separately from an interpretation?
questions.answer: The original observation and its source, time, and conditions.

questions.prompt: Two reports repeat one measurement. How many independent observations do they represent?
questions.answer: One.

questions.prompt: Why could an absence of detections be ambiguous?
questions.answer: The activity could be absent or the observing system might have had incomplete coverage.

lessons.title: Frequency, wavelength, and information on a radio wave
lessons.summary: Use wave and signal vocabulary accurately in a classroom explanation of why different systems share the electromagnetic spectrum.
objectives: Distinguish frequency, wavelength, amplitude, and polarization.
Explain why modulation and the carrying radio wave are different concepts.

sections.heading: Read the axes of a wave
sections.text: Frequency is the number of cycles per second. Wavelength is the distance between points at the same phase on neighboring cycles. In a given medium, a higher frequency corresponds to a shorter wavelength. Amplitude describes the magnitude of an oscillation. In classroom diagrams, plotting distance reveals wavelength directly, while plotting time reveals period and therefore frequency. Check which variable is on the horizontal axis before interpreting a diagram.

sections.heading: A carrier can convey a message
sections.text: Modulation varies a property of a carrier so it can represent information. In amplitude modulation, the magnitude changes in relation to the information. In frequency modulation, the instantaneous frequency changes. Pulse modulation uses characteristics of pulses to carry information. A radio-frequency band tells you the broad location of a signal in the spectrum, and other characteristics help explain how a compatible receiver interprets its information.

sections.heading: Polarization and compatibility
sections.text: Polarization characterizes the orientation and behavior of a wave's electric field. Two waves can have the same nominal frequency and different polarization. A receiver designed for one condition may respond differently to the other. When reading an equipment description, identify which properties describe the signal and which describe how the equipment interacts with it. The distinction also helps explain why two systems may interpret a shared electromagnetic environment differently.

questions.prompt: A classroom sketch shows distance between two adjacent wave crests. Which property is being measured?
questions.answer: Wavelength.

questions.prompt: Which quantity changes in amplitude modulation?
questions.answer: The carrier's amplitude varies to represent information.

questions.prompt: Two waves have equal frequency. Can their polarization differ?
questions.answer: Yes. Frequency and polarization describe different properties.

lessons.title: Why radio reception varies with the environment
lessons.summary: Use physical concepts to explain variation in reception and identify limits of an idealized radio model.
objectives: Distinguish reflection, refraction, diffraction, and multipath.
Explain why atmospheric layers may matter for different radio bands.
Explain which assumptions a technical estimate depends on and what kind of evidence could challenge them.

sections.heading: Paths through the environment
sections.text: A radio wave can follow different paths from a source to a receiver. Reflection redirects energy from a surface. Refraction changes a wave's direction as it travels through a region with changing propagation properties. Diffraction describes how waves spread around an edge or opening. A straight-line drawing is a useful starting model when the direct path dominates, and it omits other paths that may also contribute to reception.

sections.heading: Receiving more than one path
sections.text: Multipath occurs when copies of a signal reach a receiver after taking different routes. The copies can arrive with different delays and phases, which changes how they combine. A point near a reflective surface can consequently have a stronger or weaker signal than a simple distance-only prediction suggests. In a classroom example involving ordinary broadcasts, a change in sound quality from one place to another could be consistent with this phenomenon.

sections.heading: Why atmospheric layers matter
sections.text: The atmosphere is not uniform. Its lower layers and ionized regions can alter propagation in different ways, and the importance of a given layer depends on frequency and environmental conditions. Some signals can travel beyond a direct path, while other conditions favor local reception. Treat a propagation prediction as a statement about an assumed environment, and retain uncertainty when measurements provide only a partial picture.

sections.heading: Read an estimate with its assumptions
sections.text: Appendix B illustrates how a technical result depends on the assumptions behind its model. A generic radio reception model might treat a path as clear and its environment as stable. If measurements came from inside two different buildings, the apparent precision in the model output would say little about how faithfully it represents those paths. Before using an estimate, identify which assumptions describe the actual situation, which remain unverified, and whether changing one of them could change the conclusion. The study task is to interpret the limits of a model.

questions.prompt: Which term means a signal reaches a receiver along several paths?
questions.answer: Multipath.

questions.prompt: A wave spreads around the edge of a structure. Which effect describes that behavior?
questions.answer: Diffraction.

questions.prompt: Why can the same generic path model give different results on different days?
questions.answer: The atmospheric conditions and other environmental assumptions may differ.

questions.prompt: A classroom estimate assumes a clear radio path. The observation came from inside a building with several reflective surfaces. What can you conclude from a difference between the prediction and the observation?
questions.answer: The prediction and observation describe different path conditions. The discrepancy is a reason to test the clear-path assumption and compare observations from known conditions. It does not by itself identify which effect caused the difference.

lessons.title: Reporting as a coordination function
lessons.summary: Explain how interference reporting, spectrum coordination, and summary records support different staff decisions.
objectives: Choose the relevant purpose of an interference report, coordination message, or mission summary.
Identify the evidence and responsibility needed for a useful handoff.

sections.heading: Select the record by its purpose
sections.text: Appendix D collects several forms and message types used by EW personnel. An interference report documents a degradation that needs investigation. A spectrum deconfliction record communicates constraints or coordination decisions relevant to other users. A mission summary provides a record for review and assessment. The information needed for one of these records can overlap with another, but the reader's next decision gives each record a distinct purpose.

sections.heading: Make the observation usable
sections.text: When a receiver in a classroom exercise reports repeated service interruptions, the responsible staff needs the service affected, timing, scope, and status. It also needs the source of those details so that it can resolve inconsistent reports. Clear records allow successive shifts to track a continuing issue without reestablishing basic facts. Any hypothesis about a cause should carry enough context for a later reviewer to compare it with the underlying record.

sections.heading: Preserve decisions and changes
sections.text: A coordination record should make clear which stakeholders were affected by a decision and when the condition changes. A summary after an exercise can then connect observations and decisions to outcomes. If a service recovered, the summary can say when it recovered and what evidence supports that conclusion. Keeping the trail intact helps staff distinguish an actual recovery from a pause in reports.

questions.prompt: What kind of record supports investigation into unexplained service loss?
questions.answer: An interference report.

questions.prompt: Which kind of record communicates a shared spectrum constraint to affected users?
questions.answer: A spectrum deconfliction record.

questions.prompt: Which detail enables a reviewer to compare conflicting entries?
questions.answer: The source, time, and scope of each original observation.
