lessons.title: EW platoon leaders, teams, and operators
lessons.summary: Describe how leaders and teams maintain readiness and support the parent formation.
objectives: Identify key responsibilities of the platoon leader, platoon sergeant, and team chiefs.
Explain how capability limitations change a support commitment.

sections.heading: Put EW capability in context
sections.text: The EW platoon works in support of a parent formation or under a designated support relationship. The manual groups EW competencies around understanding the environment, protecting friendly people and capabilities, and delivering effects. The platoon's actual contribution depends on trained personnel, available equipment, communications, support, and authorities. Some analysis and technical support may be available through reachback, and the staff needs to know which dependencies matter for the assigned task.

sections.heading: Connect command responsibility to the work
sections.text: The platoon leader is accountable to the company commander and plans the platoon's contribution with the supported staff. The platoon sergeant supports planning and supervises readiness, sustainment, and the work of subordinate teams. Team chiefs oversee operators, equipment, and team reporting. These responsibilities overlap in practice. A team reports the impact of a maintenance problem, the platoon sergeant assesses readiness, and the platoon leader communicates how the problem affects the commitment to the supported formation.

sections.heading: Give the supported unit a reliable answer
sections.text: An equipment count shows what the platoon holds. A readiness report also accounts for whether the equipment is serviceable, operators are available, and support can be sustained. For a classroom exercise, two serviceable systems with one trained crew support a smaller commitment than the equipment count suggests. Describing that limit early gives leaders time to align priorities and make a feasible plan.

questions.prompt: Who is accountable to the company commander for the platoon?
questions.answer: The platoon leader.

questions.prompt: Which leader helps translate team maintenance reports into a platoon readiness picture?
questions.answer: The platoon sergeant.

questions.prompt: Why can a serviceable equipment count overstate available capacity?
questions.answer: Staffing, communications, sustainment, or authority may constrain what the platoon can provide.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter 1, Sections I–III, pp. 1-1 to 1-11

lessons.title: Organizational, command, and support relationships
lessons.summary: Read an Army EW organizational description and identify how command and support responsibilities differ.
objectives: Distinguish an organic organizational relationship from assigned support.
Explain what leaders clarify when a team supports another unit.

sections.heading: Read the chart with its date in mind
sections.text: The chapter describes several platoon organizations, including brigade combat team, division, corps, special forces group, and multidomain effects battalion examples. A chart identifies where the platoon is organized in that example. The unit's actual organization and attachments depend on current force structure and orders. When comparing diagrams, notice whether the platoon is shown within a company, a larger EW organization, or a specialized formation with a different purpose.

sections.heading: Ask who commands and who is supported
sections.text: A command relationship defines superior and subordinate responsibilities and associated authority. A support relationship identifies the force receiving assistance and establishes obligations for providing that support. The same team can remain under its parent command while being directed to support another unit. Leaders need a shared understanding of which organization sets priorities, how requests are coordinated, and who provides personnel and administrative support.

sections.heading: Technical control serves another purpose
sections.text: Technical control concerns the technical direction and coordination needed for a specialized function. It helps align standards and technical work across organizations. For an exercise, an EW planner might coordinate standards for observation reports while the team leader remains accountable through the platoon chain. A classroom relationship diagram becomes useful when it shows both who decides and who needs information. Orders and higher guidance settle ambiguities when relationships change.

questions.prompt: Can an EW team support another unit while remaining under its parent command?
questions.answer: Yes. The support and command relationships can coexist.

questions.prompt: Which relationship describes superior and subordinate authority?
questions.answer: The command relationship.

questions.prompt: What does technical control help coordinate?
questions.answer: The specialized standards, technical direction, and activities required for the function.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter 1, Sections IV–V, pp. 1-12 to 1-28

lessons.title: Troop-leading procedures and staff planning
lessons.summary: Explain how troop-leading procedures connect a platoon plan to a headquarters plan.
objectives: Distinguish headquarters MDMP from platoon troop-leading procedures.
Explain why a warning order and supervision support parallel preparation.

sections.heading: Parallel planning at different levels
sections.text: A headquarters staff uses the military decision-making process to help its commander build and compare courses of action. At platoon level, leaders use troop-leading procedures to understand the assignment, develop a plan, communicate it, and supervise preparation. The two processes can unfold in parallel as a platoon receives updates from the parent or supported headquarters. The platoon leader also sends concerns and changes in readiness upward to keep higher planning grounded.

sections.heading: Share what is known early
sections.text: A warning order gives subordinates time to prepare while more details are still being developed. During a training exercise, leaders can confirm personnel availability and inspect reporting equipment once they know the likely assignment. Labeling tentative information as tentative helps teams distinguish early preparation from decisions that depend on the final order. Updates should explain which assumptions changed and which preparatory work is still useful.

sections.heading: Refine the plan with evidence
sections.text: A tentative plan becomes more specific as leaders review requirements, confirm constraints, and coordinate support. The order communicates the approved plan, and supervision continues as teams prepare. If a rehearsal shows that the planned reporting relationship is unclear, the leader can clarify it and share that change with everyone affected. Reassessment continues throughout the operations process as the platoon confirms what it can deliver.

questions.prompt: What planning process is designed for use by small-unit leaders?
questions.answer: Troop-leading procedures.

questions.prompt: Why issue a warning order before the plan is complete?
questions.answer: It allows subordinate teams to begin preparation and identify issues early.

questions.prompt: A rehearsal reveals conflicting reporting expectations. What does the leader refine?
questions.answer: The information handoff and the instructions that define who receives the report.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter 2, Sections I–II, pp. 2-1 to 2-8 and 2-34 to 2-37

lessons.title: Rehearsals, checks, and collective training
lessons.summary: Plan a classroom rehearsal that checks a specific EW platoon coordination task against an observable standard.
objectives: Distinguish the purposes of rehearsals, pre-combat checks, and inspections.
Connect a training objective, evaluation, feedback, and retraining.
Explain how leaders use observed individual and collective performance to judge the scope of a readiness claim.

sections.heading: Rehearse a handoff as it happens
sections.text: A rehearsal lets teams practice how their actions and decisions connect. A tabletop report exchange can test whether team chiefs know where to route an observation and whether staff members recognize when to ask for more evidence. Give participants the actual training materials and have them carry out the handoff. A discussion of what people intend to do is useful background, while an observed rehearsal reveals timing, understanding, and coordination issues.

sections.heading: Confirm readiness through checks and inspections
sections.text: Checks confirm that personnel and equipment are ready for the assigned work. Inspections give leaders a way to verify that required standards were met and that unresolved issues are visible. For a classroom example, the checklist may cover working communications, current reference material, and the availability of forms. Match the check to the exercise objective so small administrative details do not obscure a missing prerequisite.

sections.heading: Observe, review, and train again
sections.text: The 8-step training model in the chapter provides a flexible way to plan and manage a training event. An observable objective defines what the evaluator looks for. After the event, an after-action review can identify what happened and why. If a team assigns reports correctly but omits their time reference, its follow-up practice can focus on that particular gap and verify the improvement.

sections.heading: Match the readiness claim to the evidence
sections.text: Appendix A presents tactical skills for training, while Chapter 2 explains how leaders plan, supervise, and evaluate practice. A team member who correctly explains a role has demonstrated conceptual knowledge. A team that performs an observed handoff under the conditions selected for the exercise has demonstrated a collective task under those conditions. Those are different readiness claims. If the task fails when two groups exchange information, evaluate the shared handoff and retrain it even if each person can describe their own role accurately. Practical performance belongs in supervised training.

questions.prompt: What can a rehearsal reveal about a reporting handoff?
questions.answer: Whether the right people exchange usable information at the required time.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of an inspection?
questions.answer: To verify that personnel, equipment, and preparation meet the required standards.

questions.prompt: What should happen after an evaluation finds a recurring error?
questions.answer: Identify the cause, practice the affected task, then check performance again.

questions.prompt: Everyone can explain their part of a classroom handoff, but the receiving group missed two changes during an observed rehearsal. What should the leader conclude and evaluate next?
questions.answer: Individual understanding is useful evidence. The observed errors show a gap in collective execution. Evaluate how updates are sent, received, and acknowledged during supervised practice, then check whether the handoff improves.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter 2, Sections III–IV, pp. 2-38 to 2-47; Appendix A, introduction, p. A-1

lessons.title: Platoon support across echelons and degraded conditions
lessons.summary: Describe the coordination demands of EW platoon support and what staff need to know when a service degrades.
objectives: Explain why corps, division, and brigade require different detail in support reports.
Assess a degraded-service observation for scope, certainty, and operational impact.

sections.heading: Support follows the supported formation's needs
sections.text: Corps and division staffs integrate support across multiple formations and longer planning horizons. A brigade has immediate requirements for its assigned operation and needs reports that can inform its decisions. An EW platoon works within the priorities and relationships established for its mission. A report that begins with the operational consequence makes its technical details easier for each echelon to use.

sections.heading: Preserve awareness in a contested environment
sections.text: The contested-environment section connects friendly electromagnetic protection with recognition of service losses. A communications failure may stem from unintentional interference, equipment condition, local circumstances, or hostile activity. In a training scenario, label the symptom and any possible cause separately. Determine what service users can still carry out, whether reports agree, and which decisions require an update to the supported staff.

sections.heading: Communicate what changed and what is needed
sections.text: A useful update states which service or capability changed, what the platoon can currently provide, and when the next report is due. For example, losing one exercise reporting channel may delay submission while a separate training channel remains available. The staff can then plan around the reduced capacity and assess whether priorities should change. Continuing reports help establish when the problem ends or whether its scope expands.

questions.prompt: Why can one EW observation require different summaries at brigade and division?
questions.answer: Their decisions operate at different scopes and time horizons.

questions.prompt: A service fails during an exercise. What should the initial report distinguish?
questions.answer: The observed failure, its mission impact, and any unconfirmed explanation.

questions.prompt: Which part of an update helps the supported staff decide how to respond?
questions.answer: The current operational consequence and the support the platoon can still provide.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter 3, Sections I–II, pp. 3-1, 3-11, and 3-16 to 3-17

lessons.title: Sustainment, supply, and property accountability
lessons.summary: Build a simple readiness picture from a fictional platoon's personnel, equipment, and supply needs.
objectives: Describe how the platoon leader, platoon sergeant, and teams share sustainment responsibilities.
Distinguish demand forecasts, supply reporting, and property accountability.

sections.heading: Sustainment is part of feasibility
sections.text: Readiness depends on people, serviceable equipment, and the support needed to keep them available for the duration of an assignment. A platoon leader considers that support while planning. The platoon sergeant consolidates needs and works with the supporting organization. Teams and operators keep records of consumption, equipment condition, and shortages. A recurring shortage reported late can turn a feasible task into a commitment the platoon cannot sustain.

sections.heading: Separate forecast, holdings, and responsibility
sections.text: A forecast estimates the amount of a resource needed under stated assumptions. A holdings report records what is on hand and available. Property-accountability records establish responsibility for equipment and help track changes when items move between people or organizations. The chapter distinguishes expendable property consumed in use, durable property controlled by the user, and nonexpendable property requiring formal accounting. In a training exercise, three teams may need supplies for the same duration while holding different amounts. A useful summary shows each shortfall and the assumptions that produced the forecast.

sections.heading: Plan with conditions and priorities
sections.text: The sustainment plan ties demand to the timing of the supported activity and identifies what is needed from outside the platoon. Load planning and onboard spares matter because availability can change after preparation ends. A report should explain how a shortfall affects readiness and when it will first matter. If the training schedule changes, leaders update the affected assumptions and communicate the new requirement through the support chain.

questions.prompt: Which report describes what is actually on hand?
questions.answer: A holdings or supply-status report.

questions.prompt: Why identify assumptions behind a supply forecast?
questions.answer: So leaders can revise the estimate when duration, consumption, or activity changes.

questions.prompt: What connects a shortage to a decision?
questions.answer: Its expected time and impact on readiness or the supported activity.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter 4, Sections I–II, pp. 4-1 to 4-9

lessons.title: Maintenance and readiness reporting
lessons.summary: Explain how preventive maintenance, repair, and reporting support availability over time.
objectives: Distinguish preventive checks, repair responsibility, and readiness reporting.
State what an equipment-status update should communicate to the supported unit.

sections.heading: Availability changes over time
sections.text: Equipment that is serviceable when an exercise begins may develop a fault later. Preventive checks and routine servicing make problems visible while there is time to address them. Operators are close to the equipment and can report what changed. Team and platoon leaders supervise maintenance and coordinate issues requiring support beyond their level. Leaders use these records to understand available capability for the current task and the next one.

sections.heading: Give the support chain a usable record
sections.text: In a training scenario, an operator who reports that a device is intermittent should describe the symptom, when it occurred, and which functions remain usable. The maintenance organization can use those observations when it assesses the fault. The supported unit needs the effect on service and anticipated update time. A single record can support both uses by separating technical observations from the readiness judgment.

sections.heading: Follow through on repair and resupply
sections.text: Resupply and maintenance may be coordinated through different channels, and both change the readiness picture. An ordered part changes the forecast, and the affected equipment remains subject to its recorded status until the repair is verified. Once repair and readiness are confirmed, staff can revise the support commitment. Keeping the current status, responsible organization, and next review time visible reduces duplicate requests and helps leaders see patterns that require changes to preparation or sustainment.

terms: PMCS — preventive maintenance checks and services

questions.prompt: Who first observes many equipment faults?
questions.answer: The teams and operators who use the equipment.

questions.prompt: What does the supported formation need to know about a maintenance issue?
questions.answer: The effect on support, what capability remains available, and when the status will be updated.

questions.prompt: When should an organization count repaired equipment as available?
questions.answer: When serviceability and readiness have been confirmed.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter 4, Section II, pp. 4-9 and 4-13 to 4-15

lessons.title: What belongs in the electromagnetic operating picture?
lessons.summary: Distinguish the spectrum itself, radiation already present, and conditions that can affect spectrum-dependent work.
objectives: Distinguish EMS, EME and EMOE
Recognize how geography, time and expected use change an EMOE estimate

sections.heading: The spectrum and the environment
sections.text: The electromagnetic spectrum (EMS) encompasses frequencies from radio waves through visible light and beyond. The electromagnetic environment (EME) is the electromagnetic energy a system actually encounters in its surroundings. That environment can change even when a receiver stays in one place. A nearby transmitter might switch on later in the day, or a storm might change the background conditions.

sections.heading: The environment relevant to a decision
sections.text: The electromagnetic operational environment (EMOE) adds the conditions and potential sources that matter to the activity under consideration. It includes systems that may start transmitting, receivers that must keep working, and natural or man-made factors such as terrain, weather and noise. The same physical area can therefore have different implications for teams supporting different services or operating at different times.

sections.heading: A shared festival site
sections.text: In the morning, a venue team observes little radio traffic. During the event, volunteer groups, a neighboring station and ambulance crews will use separate equipment. The morning sample is evidence about the EME at one time. A useful EMOE estimate also accounts for expected users, the service that must stay available, the layout of the venue and the period that the sample represents. The estimate should distinguish confirmed observations from assumptions about later activity.

questions.prompt: What does an EME observation describe?
questions.answer: Electromagnetic energy actually encountered at a stated place and time.

questions.prompt: Why can a silent system belong in an EMOE estimate?
questions.answer: Its future transmission or its need to receive can affect the activity being planned.

questions.prompt: A morning survey is quiet before a busy afternoon festival. Is it sufficient to describe the afternoon EMOE?
questions.answer: No. Record the measured period and add expected afternoon users, receiving needs and uncertainty.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter I, §1.b (I-1–I-5), figure I-1

lessons.title: How spectrum use supports joint functions
lessons.summary: Connect spectrum access and electromagnetic warfare categories to the broader joint framework.
objectives: Explain how JEMSO connects spectrum-dependent mission areas
Distinguish electromagnetic attack, protection and support at the definition level
Recognize spectrum dependencies across joint functions

sections.heading: A framework spanning functions
sections.text: Joint electromagnetic spectrum operations (JEMSO) coordinate use of the electromagnetic operational environment across components and mission areas. The seven joint functions in this edition are command and control, intelligence, fires, movement and maneuver, protection, sustainment, and information. A communications failure can cross several of these boundaries because multiple functions can depend on the same link, sensing service, or timing source.

sections.heading: Three electromagnetic warfare categories
sections.text: Electromagnetic warfare (EW) is one contributor to JEMSO. Electromagnetic attack concerns the application of electromagnetic effects against an adversary. Electromagnetic protection concerns maintaining friendly capability in the presence of electromagnetic effects. Electromagnetic support concerns recognizing and interpreting emissions for immediate operational awareness. Spectrum management coordinates access and limits conflicts. Intelligence, cyberspace and space organizations contribute their own authorities or capabilities where systems and dependencies overlap.

sections.heading: Follow a shared dependency
sections.text: At a port safety exercise, dispatch, the inspection team and a supply contractor all depend on timely position reports. If a provider supplying that data loses service, switching the dispatch radio alone may leave the other groups without the information they need. Drawing the dependency from each team to the shared service gives coordinators a clearer picture of who needs to participate in planning and who must be informed of a change.

questions.prompt: Is spectrum management synonymous with EW in the 2020 framework?
questions.answer: No. They contribute distinct functions that JEMSO integrates with intelligence and other mission areas.

questions.prompt: Which EW category addresses the continued functioning of friendly systems amid electromagnetic effects?
questions.answer: Electromagnetic protection.

questions.prompt: Dispatch and supply logistics use the same position reporting service. What should a spectrum planner record?
questions.answer: The shared dependency and the functions that would be affected by loss of the service.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter I, §1.c–d (I-5–I-11) and §3 (I-12–I-14); Appendix B, §2 (B-1–B-2), category headings

lessons.title: Compatibility, interference and environmental effects
lessons.summary: Separate system performance and safety hazards from assumptions about the source of a disturbance.
objectives: Explain electromagnetic environmental effects and compatibility
Distinguish interference, a pulse and radiation safety hazards
Identify what to record when a system degrades

sections.heading: What environmental effects cover
sections.text: Electromagnetic environmental effects (E3) describe how the surrounding electromagnetic environment changes the performance of equipment, systems or people supporting an activity. Electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) is the ability of systems to operate together with acceptable performance. It depends on the environment in which systems operate. Compatibility established in one setting can fail in another if different equipment or environmental conditions are present.

sections.heading: Separate kinds of problems
sections.text: Electromagnetic interference (EMI) is a disturbance that degrades a system. It can result from ordinary equipment interaction or intentional activity. The symptom by itself does not establish which. Electromagnetic pulse refers to a brief, intense electromagnetic disturbance that can couple into electronics. Radio-frequency exposure hazards concern safety around personnel, sensitive equipment or certain operations. Safety reviews apply established limits and approved guidance.

sections.heading: Describe observations first
sections.text: In a demonstration hall, a wireless status display becomes unreliable when more exhibitors arrive. That observation makes coexistence worth reviewing. The event team should preserve when and where the symptom occurred, which service degraded and whether performance changed with the local environment. If there is a potential exposure issue, the safety lead handles it through established controls. The diagnosis should preserve other explanations until the evidence supports one.

questions.prompt: What property does electromagnetic compatibility describe?
questions.answer: The ability of systems to work in their environment without unacceptable interference or degradation.

questions.prompt: Does a loss of reception establish that someone intentionally interfered?
questions.answer: No. Interference can be intentional or unintentional, and other causes of loss still need to be considered.

questions.prompt: A display fails only during a crowded demonstration. What should the event team document first?
questions.answer: Time, location, affected service, symptoms and surrounding conditions, with any suspected cause labelled as a hypothesis.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter I, §2 (I-11–I-12) and §1 (I-2–I-5)

lessons.title: Command authority and cross-component coordination
lessons.summary: Trace who sets priorities, who coordinates shared spectrum, and who carries out component responsibilities.
objectives: Differentiate the JFC, EMSCA and JEMSOC
Explain why component liaisons matter in centralized coordination
Identify when a conflict needs higher-level resolution

sections.heading: The decision chain
sections.text: The joint force commander (JFC) sets command-specific policy and priorities and is responsible for how the joint force is organized. The electromagnetic spectrum coordinating authority (EMSCA) is a designated authority whose responsibilities include coordinating, prioritizing and assessing JEMSO. The 2020 text describes typical delegation arrangements and allows the commander to adapt them to the mission and staff available.

sections.heading: The coordinating cell
sections.text: The joint electromagnetic spectrum operations cell (JEMSOC) brings together people who can represent component requirements and relevant staff functions. It connects operations, spectrum management, intelligence and other subject-matter expertise so that they can use a shared picture and address competing needs. A cell has to understand which decisions it can make under delegated authority and which ones require approval.

sections.heading: Central agreement and local work
sections.text: A joint training event needs reliable radio service for medical staff and several training groups. Each group knows its own requirements and retains responsibility for its approved activity. The coordination cell can identify that two groups’ needs overlap, ask them to clarify timing and explain the trade-off. An unresolved priority decision belongs with the appropriate authority. The cell then communicates the approved decision across the affected groups.

questions.prompt: What does the JFC provide at the start?
questions.answer: Command policy, objectives and priorities, with organizational arrangements and assigned authorities.

questions.prompt: Why include component liaisons in a joint cell?
questions.answer: They convey component requirements and constraints and carry decisions and updates back to the component.

questions.prompt: Two groups cannot agree on use of a shared resource. What should the cell bring to the appropriate authority?
questions.answer: Both requirements, the conflict and its service effects, feasible alternatives and the decision needed.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter II, §§1–3 (II-1–II-17), figures II-1–II-3

lessons.title: Service, intelligence and external support
lessons.summary: Understand why the joint staff relies on distinct component, intelligence and specialist organizations.
objectives: Describe what components contribute to joint coordination
Recognize the specialist organizations in Appendix D
Identify a useful request for specialist support

sections.heading: One plan, different organizations
sections.text: Services organize spectrum work around their own missions and staff structures. The joint staff needs component input to understand realistic requirements, current constraints and the implications of changes. Liaisons and shared definitions make distinct structures usable together. Multinational arrangements can use a coordination cell with different terminology and responsibilities. The relevant question is which authority or staff function a group actually performs.

sections.heading: Specialists add a different layer
sections.text: Joint intelligence staff coordinates the intelligence contribution. Theater and national organizations can fill information gaps outside a component’s reach. Appendix D describes United States Strategic Command support in the 2020 organization, Joint Navigation Warfare Center support on positioning, navigation and timing, and Joint Spectrum Center spectrum engineering and analytical support. Those descriptions refer to the organizations and mandates in the source edition.

sections.heading: Frame a request around the decision
sections.text: At a multiagency exercise, two organizations report incompatible timestamps from different position reporting sources. An effective support request describes the observed inconsistency, the services affected, which records can be shared and the choice the exercise directors need to make. The component provides local evidence. The coordinating staff identifies the specialist who can evaluate the dependency and makes sure the answer reaches the groups that need it.

questions.prompt: Why does a joint staff need Service component representation?
questions.answer: Components bring equipment and task knowledge, local constraints and changes that a central staff may not see.

questions.prompt: Which Appendix D organization focuses on navigation-related support?
questions.answer: The Joint Navigation Warfare Center.

questions.prompt: A practice exercise has inconsistent timestamps from several systems. What makes a support request actionable?
questions.answer: State what differs, why it matters, what evidence is available, what is shareable and what decision needs support.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter II, §§4–6 (II-17–II-24); Appendix D, Annexes A–C

lessons.title: From planning guidance to a coordinated appendix
lessons.summary: Track how spectrum constraints enter joint planning, shape options and carry forward into an approved plan.
objectives: Identify the purpose of the JEMSO staff estimate
Describe how component inputs shape a joint plan
Distinguish an estimate from the JEMSO appendix
Explain how a shared constraint affects a comparison of alternatives and which information should carry into the approved plan.

sections.heading: Start with the decision
sections.text: Spectrum considerations belong in the joint planning process from mission analysis onward. At this stage the staff identifies dependencies, available access, potential conflicts and uncertainties. The JEMSO staff estimate summarizes the spectrum aspects of the situation and how they affect the alternatives under consideration. As assumptions change or stronger evidence arrives, the estimate is updated.

sections.heading: Carry decisions into the plan
sections.text: The JEMSOC brings component requirements together under command guidance. During comparison of courses of action, the staff considers which option the available spectrum resources can support and the remaining risks. In this edition the selected course of action informs the JEMSO appendix to Annex C of the joint plan. The appendix records the coordinated arrangement and associated responsibilities. The estimate explains the evidence and choices behind it.

sections.heading: Example from a civil exercise
sections.text: An exercise director is comparing a single site with two smaller sites. Planners identify the same dispatch and medical coordination needs in both cases. At the split sites, the teams also need to communicate across venues. If reliable cross-site communication is unconfirmed, the estimate identifies that uncertainty in the comparison. Once the director selects a plan, the published arrangement records approved responsibilities, contacts and how the parties learn of changes.

sections.heading: Compare alternatives by the same requirement
sections.text: Chapter III and Appendix G connect mission analysis to a comparison of alternatives. First state the requirement that all alternatives must satisfy. Then show where the evidence differs and name which assumptions could change the recommendation. In a joint exercise, two components may both list a shared service as available because each checked it independently. Once their schedules are compared, the overlapping use becomes a joint coordination issue. The estimate should explain how the conflict affects each alternative, and the published appendix should record the selected arrangement and who is responsible for it.

questions.prompt: When should spectrum considerations enter joint planning?
questions.answer: During mission analysis, then throughout development, analysis and comparison of alternatives and preparation of the plan.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes the staff estimate from the published JEMSO appendix?
questions.answer: The estimate analyzes requirements, risks and options. The appendix carries the coordinated decisions into the plan.

questions.prompt: An event alternative assumes reliable cross-site service that has not been confirmed. What belongs in the estimate?
questions.answer: The dependency, supporting evidence, uncertainty and consequence if the assumption is wrong.

questions.prompt: Two exercise alternatives both show a shared service as available. Only one requires both components to use it at the same time, and concurrent use is unverified. What belongs in the estimate, and what belongs in the published appendix after selection?
questions.answer: The estimate compares both alternatives against the same service requirement, states the unresolved concurrent-use assumption, and explains its effect on supportability. The published appendix records the selected arrangement, responsibilities and any surviving dependency that must be tracked.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter III, §§1–3 (III-1–III-17), figure III-1; Appendix C, §2 (C-1–C-6); Appendix G, §§1–2 (G-1)

lessons.title: Host nations, multinational partners and civil responders
lessons.summary: Identify the permissions and information-sharing decisions needed when several jurisdictions participate.
objectives: Explain the purpose of established host-nation coordination channels
Identify multinational data-sharing and interoperability barriers
Relate domestic spectrum coordination to civil authority relationships

sections.heading: Permission follows jurisdiction
sections.text: Host-nation coordination seeks permission for spectrum-dependent activity inside another country’s jurisdiction. The 2020 doctrine describes use of established coordination channels, often through a joint frequency management office. Planners need to understand the host’s allocation rules and service protections, as well as the approvals relevant to the proposed activity. A technical capability and permission to operate it answer different questions.

sections.heading: Agree on what partners can share
sections.text: Multinational participants may use different tools, terminology, data standards and training. Security and disclosure rules determine which records may be shared. Early guidance from the appropriate disclosure staff helps partners define a shared set of information. Coordination remains important between adjacent participants because radio propagation and service dependencies can cross an organizational boundary.

sections.heading: Domestic interoperability
sections.text: During a domestic support exercise, civil authorities and first responders may have different radio governance, request channels and communications plans. A useful shared arrangement records which organization holds authority for each resource and who updates the other parties. For example, a flood drill could include municipal responders, a federal team and a state agency. Exercise organizers can confirm the contact chain, the information everyone can use, and where an access question needs to be resolved.

questions.prompt: Why use established host-nation channels?
questions.answer: They connect the request to the lawful authority and make coordination consistent with existing agreements and relationships.

questions.prompt: What should be decided early about a proposed shared spectrum record?
questions.answer: What its fields mean, which participants can receive them and what format they can all use.

questions.prompt: Several agencies plan a flood drill in neighboring counties. Who needs to know about a resource change?
questions.answer: The responsible authorities and affected participants in both counties, through the agreed coordination channels.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter III, §§3.a, 4–5 (III-10–III-11, III-17–III-22)

lessons.title: Updates during a shared spectrum exercise
lessons.summary: Trace how a coordinated plan remains usable as participating teams report changes and new requirements.
objectives: Explain why a coordination cycle repeats
Describe how a new request affects a shared plan
Distinguish a monitoring observation from an approved change

sections.heading: Turn guidance into a common plan
sections.text: Chapter IV describes a repeating cycle. The commander sets priorities, components prepare requirements and draft plans, and the JEMSOC consolidates them for review and approval. The approved guidance gives components a common basis for their own activity. The pace of updates depends on how quickly conditions change and how the work of affected teams is scheduled.

sections.heading: Keep decisions and observations distinct
sections.text: During an exercise, participating teams can discover conflicts and report new requirements. The coordination cell reviews implications, confirms which participants are affected and obtains approval where needed. Observations also help refine the estimate of the environment. Keeping a record of the observation, pending decision and approved change helps prevent teams from treating an unreviewed request as permission.

sections.heading: A revised practice schedule
sections.text: A weekend exercise extends a demonstration into a time that a second team expected to use a shared communications service. The first team provides the revised time and its service need. Central coordination checks the conflict, discusses the trade-off with both teams and records the approved arrangement. Before relying on it, each participating group can confirm receipt of the same revision. The next cycle can use feedback on whether the agreement preserved service.

questions.prompt: Why is the execution cycle repeated?
questions.answer: Actual conditions, requirements and priorities change. The joint staff uses observations and feedback to update coordination.

questions.prompt: What is the role of component plans before joint approval?
questions.answer: They describe component requirements and proposed activities so the staff can identify conflicts and dependencies.

questions.prompt: A team asks to extend a practice slot into another team’s time. What should happen before it treats the new slot as approved?
questions.answer: The coordinating staff should review and resolve the conflict under the appropriate authority, then communicate the decision to the affected teams.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter IV, §2 (IV-1–IV-4), figure IV-1

lessons.title: Measure the work and the result
lessons.summary: Use measures of performance and effectiveness to evaluate coordinated spectrum use and update the next plan.
objectives: Distinguish performance and effectiveness measures
Use observed results to test a planning assumption
State an actionable lesson learned
Explain why a reported result needs both comparable evidence and an explicit interpretation of uncertainty.

sections.heading: Two questions for assessment
sections.text: A measure of performance asks whether the planned action took place. A measure of effectiveness asks whether the intended outcome occurred. For a shared communications exercise, sending a revised coordination notice before the start is a performance measure. Whether every participating group can exchange its required messages during the event is an effectiveness measure. The two measures can point in different directions.

sections.heading: Tie the result to evidence
sections.text: The JEMSOC aggregates component feedback and assesses it against the measures established during planning. An assessment is stronger when it gives the planned threshold, the observation period, the evidence collected and potential limits of the evidence. A change in one outcome can have several causes. Compare observations with previous periods or other relevant records before attributing the outcome to new guidance.

sections.heading: Make the review reusable
sections.text: Suppose notices went out on schedule but one desk missed several routine test calls. Record the missed calls as an outcome, the completed notices as an activity, and the available evidence about receipt and device readiness. If the evidence shows one team received an outdated version, a useful lesson would specify who should confirm the current version and when the confirmation should be captured. Review the change on the next exercise.

sections.heading: Check whether the result answers the question
sections.text: Chapter IV separates the assessment of actions from assessment of changes in conditions. In a training exercise, the staff records that an updated procedure was issued to all groups. Later, a summary says that fewer reports were lost. Before accepting an improvement claim, compare the same kind of reporting periods, check whether participation changed, and look for other changes in the exercise that could explain the result. If the groups used different logging methods, state that limitation and propose a comparable observation. A useful assessment gives the decision-maker both the most defensible conclusion and a way to test it.

questions.prompt: Is timely distribution of a notice a performance or effectiveness measure?
questions.answer: Performance. It shows whether the planned distribution step occurred.

questions.prompt: What makes an effectiveness measure useful?
questions.answer: It ties an observable outcome and threshold to the intended objective.

questions.prompt: Every team received the update, but test calls still failed. What can the review conclude?
questions.answer: Distribution was completed and the outcome fell short. Additional evidence is needed to attribute the failure.

questions.prompt: An exercise reports that all teams received a new process and that fewer reports were lost. Half the teams used no logs during the second exercise. Which conclusion is supported and how could the staff test effectiveness?
questions.answer: Distribution is evidenced as performance. The change in lost reports is inconclusive because observation coverage changed. Collect comparable logs from the same participating groups, track the number of reports sent and received, and explain remaining differences.

lessons.title: Allocation, assignment and spectrum supportability
lessons.summary: Understand how international coordination, national authorities, equipment reviews and individual permissions relate.
objectives: Distinguish allocation from assignment
Explain why equipment spectrum supportability and a local assignment are distinct
Identify the roles of international and national spectrum governance

sections.heading: From rules to particular uses
sections.text: International coordination through the International Telecommunication Union establishes frameworks for shared use across borders. Domestic authorities apply national law and manage spectrum use in their jurisdiction. In the United States, the 2020 appendix discusses the role of the National Telecommunications and Information Administration for federal use and the Federal Communications Commission for nonfederal use. Use abroad requires coordination under the relevant sovereign authority.

sections.heading: Different decisions about access
sections.text: An allocation identifies a band for a category of service. A frequency assignment authorizes a station to use a frequency or channel under defined conditions. Equipment certification and spectrum supportability address whether a proposed system can be accommodated in the governing spectrum framework and environment. Planning must account for these decisions separately because the equipment review and the specific operating authorization can have different conditions.

sections.heading: A purchasing decision
sections.text: A public research group is considering a radio telemetry system for a field study. Procurement can ask early whether the equipment is suitable for the intended service and whether appropriate access can be obtained where the study will run. The team also needs to verify the authorization applicable to its use and time period. Finding a service listed in an allocation table is one part of that inquiry.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes an allocation from an assignment?
questions.answer: Allocation designates spectrum for a category of service. An assignment authorizes a particular station’s use under specified conditions.

questions.prompt: Which two U.S. agencies does the appendix distinguish?
questions.answer: NTIA for federal spectrum use and FCC for nonfederal spectrum use.

questions.prompt: A service is allocated spectrum in a proposed study area. Does the allocation give a new research unit authority to transmit?
questions.answer: No. It still needs to identify and satisfy the operating authorization and equipment requirements applicable to the proposed use.

lessons.title: Governance for changes to spectrum-dependent systems
lessons.summary: Use a public doctrine example to understand responsibility, testing and inter-component communication when system behavior changes.
objectives: Identify who owns reprogramming in the 2020 doctrinal model
Explain why changes need coordination across components
Describe evidence that supports a controlled release

sections.heading: Name the owner and the affected users
sections.text: Appendix E places responsibility for electromagnetic warfare reprogramming with the respective Services and their support programs. It groups changes into tactics, software and hardware, and discusses joint coordination. The governance principle is that the owner evaluates and implements a proposed change while the joint staff helps account for dependencies and effects that cross components.

sections.heading: Separate evidence and approval
sections.text: Observation of a problem starts a review. A useful change record describes the observed behavior, the components affected, the evidence for the change and how it will be checked. Validation records are especially important when several groups rely on consistent behavior. Record who approves a version and communicates its adoption. Otherwise, different teams can rely on incompatible expectations about the same system.

sections.heading: A benign software example
sections.text: Several laboratories share an RF monitoring dashboard. A new dashboard version revises how the timestamp of a measurement appears. The application owner verifies the update on a representative record and checks whether other teams still interpret the output correctly. The coordinating group communicates the change and the version used in the next joint review. The teams preserve the evidence needed to explain results generated before and after the update.

questions.prompt: Who owns EW reprogramming in this edition?
questions.answer: Each Service through its reprogramming support program, with coordination across affected joint organizations.

questions.prompt: What broad categories of changes does the appendix name?
questions.answer: Tactics, software and hardware.

questions.prompt: A laboratory dashboard changes how it reports timestamps. What should the team confirm before coordinated adoption?
questions.answer: Verify representative data, check the interpretation across teams and communicate which version affected users should expect.

lessons.title: Coordination measures for shared spectrum
lessons.summary: Read reservation, restriction and control measures as rules protecting simultaneous access and safety.
objectives: Identify the dimensions used to define coordination measures
Distinguish an allotment plan from a specific assignment
Explain how a coordination rule prevents inadvertent conflicts

sections.heading: Define a rule precisely
sections.text: The appendix describes spectrum coordination measures as rules and mechanisms that are defined in dimensions such as space, time, frequency, power and waveform. These dimensions explain who can use a resource and which conditions are part of the agreement. Coordination rules can reserve resources, restrict use, identify resources available with lower conflict risk, or control actions of specified users.

sections.heading: Reserve resources and record specific use
sections.text: An allotment plan sets aside bands or groups of frequencies for an organization or function. A particular assignment defines use by an individual station or other specific user under applicable constraints. Both help coordinate use. The allotment helps allocate responsibility within a plan, and the assignment gives the individual user a clearer set of operating conditions.

sections.heading: A shared test facility
sections.text: A university facility gives two research groups access to a demonstration hall and protects a third group’s scheduled measurement window. A useful coordination record states which service is reserved, when the restriction applies, what location it covers and who may approve exceptions. The record should be shared with each affected group before the demonstrations begin. If the venue or schedule changes, review the scope of the existing permission and notify anyone newly affected.

questions.prompt: Which dimensions can define the scope of an EMS coordination measure?
questions.answer: Space, time, frequency, power and waveform are the dimensions named in Appendix F.

questions.prompt: What does an allotment plan set aside?
questions.answer: Frequency bands or groups for a designated organization or function.

questions.prompt: A protected test moves to another room and time. What should change in the shared coordination record?
questions.answer: Review and update the spatial and time boundaries, then communicate the approved update to affected users.

lessons.title: Write an estimate someone can decide from
lessons.summary: Build a concise analysis of requirements, alternatives, uncertainty and a recommendation.
objectives: Identify the main parts of a JEMSO staff estimate
Compare supportability of two alternatives
Explain why a recommendation should include residual risk

sections.heading: Describe the problem and its boundaries
sections.text: The staff estimate starts with the mission and the situation. It records requirements, available resources, constraints and assumptions that influence the decision. It then considers the courses of action in terms of spectrum support. The template asks analysts to explain how the situation can affect each option. Separating observed conditions from assumptions lets a reader see which conclusions might change.

sections.heading: Use the same criteria for each option
sections.text: The appendix emphasizes comparing courses of action and recommending which can be supported. For comparison, define a few criteria the reviewer can apply consistently, such as reliable service for each required group, dependencies that have confirmed authorization, and time needed to resolve remaining issues. A recommendation should show the reason an option ranks higher and identify risks that remain if the option is selected.

sections.heading: Example of a short estimate
sections.text: A fair can place two booths together or across separate buildings. Both layouts need access to one shared reporting service. The combined layout has verified local coverage. The separate layout is feasible only if the destination confirms coverage. The estimate can recommend the combined layout given the present evidence and explain what new evidence would make the second option supportable. That gives the decision maker a usable recommendation and a reason for revisiting it.

questions.prompt: Why state assumptions separately from verified conditions?
questions.answer: Readers can see which uncertainties might change the conclusion and which dependencies need confirmation.

questions.prompt: What should accompany an estimate’s recommendation?
questions.answer: Which alternatives can be supported, the reasons for choosing one, and the unresolved risks or requirements.

questions.prompt: Option B needs coverage that has yet to be measured. How should the estimate describe it?
questions.answer: List coverage as an unresolved dependency and identify how its confirmation would affect supportability.

lessons.title: Choose planning tools by the question they answer
lessons.summary: Distinguish databases, workflow aids and simulations and judge the evidence each can supply.
objectives: Describe three categories of planning aids in Appendix H
Recognize why source, age and permissions matter for planning data
Match a generic tool category to a planning question

sections.heading: Three tool categories
sections.text: The 2020 doctrine groups planning tools into databases, planning process aids, and modeling and simulation. Databases store relevant technical or administrative records. Workflow tools help assemble plans and manage actions. Models estimate how conditions might affect system behavior, often using geographic information. One program may combine several functions, so identify which part of it produced a particular result.

sections.heading: Check the records before relying on a tool
sections.text: The document stresses understanding the source and suitability of data. A useful review records who supplied the information, when it was checked, what period and area it represents, and which groups can access it. Two spreadsheets can both look current while covering different sites. A tool may still produce a polished map from stale or incomplete records.

sections.heading: Choose evidence that fits
sections.text: A venue planner wants to answer three questions. The equipment inventory can answer what the teams have reported. The workflow record can show whether the coordinator approved a shared resource. A model estimates whether a service might reach a new hall. In each case the answer’s reliability depends on the provenance and quality of the inputs. A critical modeled result can also be compared with a representative independent observation.

questions.prompt: Which category provides technical records for analysis?
questions.answer: A database. The analyst still checks provenance, currency and suitability.

questions.prompt: What question suits a planning process aid?
questions.answer: Where a coordination action stands, who owns it, or which approved record should be published.

questions.prompt: A map assumes that a renovated hall has its old layout. What should the planner do with the result?
questions.answer: Treat the estimate as conditional, update or verify the layout, and check the result against relevant observations.

lessons.title: Verification, validation and useful model fidelity
lessons.summary: Decide how much detail a spectrum model needs and what evidence supports its conclusions.
objectives: Distinguish model verification from validation
Explain how decision stakes and data quality affect useful fidelity
Identify a meaningful check on a model’s prediction

sections.heading: Set the fidelity for the decision
sections.text: Fidelity is the detail and accuracy with which a model represents objects, the environment and their interactions. A model for screening candidate sites may need less detail than one informing an expensive equipment acceptance decision. Available data, time, intended use and the consequences of error matter. Adding detail with weak input data may increase the effort required without producing a reliable increase in accuracy.

sections.heading: Check the model in two ways
sections.text: Verification asks whether the model functions as designed. Code and calculation reviews, controlled test cases and tests of sensitivity to inputs help check that. Validation examines how well the representation matches reality for the intended use. Observations, laboratory or field testing and comparison with trusted evidence can reveal limitations that verification alone leaves open.

sections.heading: Describe uncertainty in the result
sections.text: A university team uses a propagation model to assess whether lab telemetry is likely to work between rooms. A known test calculation can show that the model combines inputs as specified. Measurements in representative locations test the fidelity of the building and signal assumptions. If the results disagree in several rooms, report where and how they diverge and consider whether the model is fit for the specific choice under review.

questions.prompt: What does verification establish?
questions.answer: Whether the implementation behaves according to its intended logic and calculations.

questions.prompt: What does validation test?
questions.answer: Whether the model agrees with relevant observations or other credible evidence closely enough for its intended use.

questions.prompt: A model passes its calculation tests but consistently overestimates coverage in the building. Which check exposed the shortfall?
questions.answer: Validation against measurements. The implementation tests alone established only verification.

lessons.title: Congestion, constraints and the operating environment
lessons.summary: Explain why spectrum access changes with local devices, propagation conditions, civil use and authorizations.
objectives: Distinguish congestion, contest and external constraints
Recognize terrain, weather, lighting and civil sources as planning inputs
Identify information needed for a useful local inventory

sections.heading: Sources of pressure on access
sections.text: Congestion occurs when multiple devices compete for portions of the spectrum at the same time. A contested environment includes deliberate efforts to disrupt access. Policy, assignments and protections for other services can also constrain access. A practical planning picture distinguishes these conditions because each calls for different evidence. A crowded environment alone provides little basis for attributing a fault to deliberate action.

sections.heading: Physical and civil conditions
sections.text: Terrain and buildings may obstruct or reflect energy. Weather and atmospheric conditions can alter propagation. Optical systems also depend on illumination. Civil infrastructure, licensed services and locally purchased equipment may add dependencies or interference sources. Include both equipment that transmits and services that require reliable reception when building the local inventory.

sections.heading: A local equipment survey
sections.text: A training site is adding telemetry for a safety drill. The inventory should include existing facility systems, temporary equipment from participating groups, relevant civilian services and receivers that need protection from interference. Planners record which devices are known to be present, when they operate and which details still need verification. The owner and last confirmed date help when two groups supply conflicting records. A review can then connect changes in expected conditions to possible effects on the exercise.

questions.prompt: How does congestion arise?
questions.answer: Several devices attempt to use overlapping spectrum resources at the same time.

questions.prompt: Why inventory receivers as well as transmitters?
questions.answer: Receivers enable dependent services and can suffer interference even when they emit no signal.

questions.prompt: A building wall was added after an earlier exercise. Why revisit the spectrum plan?
questions.answer: The new structure can affect propagation, so earlier coverage or coexistence observations may have limited applicability.

lessons.title: Four core functions and three recurring activities
lessons.summary: Use the Army’s terminology to connect user requirements, authorization, partnership and policy.
objectives: Name the four Army spectrum management operations functions
Distinguish core functions from planning, coordinating and managing activities
Explain how requirements and resources move between echelons

sections.heading: Four core functions
sections.text: ATP 6-02.70 describes four interrelated core functions. Spectrum management handles engineering, administrative and coordination work. Frequency assignment authorizes a particular use under defined conditions. Host-nation coordination addresses permission from the sovereign authority concerned. Policy provides the rules that guide those decisions. A manager may draw on all four functions while supporting a single request.

sections.heading: Three recurring activities
sections.text: The manual describes planning, coordinating and managing as recurring activities. Planning identifies requirements and constraints. Coordination brings together staff, spectrum users and partners to resolve conflicts. Management maintains records, relationships and resource use as conditions change. Requirements come from the units with a specific need, while resources and policy guidance are often provided through higher echelons.

sections.heading: Apply the terms to one request
sections.text: An installation group asks to use a wireless reporting system during an exercise. It describes the service needed, relevant equipment and period of use. The spectrum manager reviews existing authorizations and local constraints, consults affected users and arranges the proper assignment or approval. If another tenant has a conflicting need, the manager asks which policy or designated authority resolves the overlap. The inventory and coordination records provide evidence for later users and help identify overlaps if the exercise expands.

questions.prompt: What are the Army’s four core functions?
questions.answer: Spectrum management, frequency assignment, host-nation coordination and policy.

questions.prompt: Why describe requirements as bottom-driven and resources as top-fed?
questions.answer: Users describe what they need. Higher authorities provide or coordinate resources and policy within their jurisdiction.

questions.prompt: A training team extends its event after receiving an assignment with a fixed end time. Which activities are needed?
questions.answer: Update the planned requirement, coordinate with affected users and the proper authority, and record the resulting decision.

lessons.title: Who owns the spectrum question at each echelon?
lessons.summary: Trace a requirement or an interference report from a unit through installation, theater and corps-level support.
objectives: Identify installation and theater spectrum management responsibilities
Explain how corps, division and brigade responsibilities connect
Distinguish signal staff and CEMA coordination responsibilities at a conceptual level

sections.heading: Installation and theater
sections.text: The installation spectrum manager is a central point for tenants, training units and local spectrum use. This role maintains installation records, checks authorizations and processes requests. The theater Army spectrum manager handles theater policy and coordinates with regulatory and host-nation authorities. Theater signal brigades and expeditionary signal battalions support communications and contribute requirements from their networks and users.

sections.heading: Corps through brigade
sections.text: The corps establishes policies and procedures for subordinate use and helps secure resources. Division spectrum staff coordinates across subordinate organizations, manages records and elevates unresolved problems. Brigade staff needs accurate records of its devices and requirements and coordinates with its supporting organization. Signal staff handles communications and spectrum coordination. CEMA staff contributes spectrum awareness and cross-functional coordination for cyberspace and electromagnetic warfare activities.

sections.heading: Escalate with a complete record
sections.text: At a training site, a visiting group and the facility staff both report intermittent loss of service. The group can document symptoms and give its inventory to the installation manager for local coordination. If the issue spans adjacent units or cannot be resolved locally, the record can move through the responsible higher staff. The next echelon needs the observations, affected organizations, actions already taken and the pending decision.

questions.prompt: What does an installation spectrum manager do for tenant activities?
questions.answer: Keeps records, explains local rules, checks authorization conditions and processes or forwards requests.

questions.prompt: Why do units keep device inventories?
questions.answer: Higher staffs depend on accurate requirements and equipment data to coordinate resources and assess interference.

questions.prompt: Two adjacent units report the same reception problem. What information should accompany escalation?
questions.answer: Affected services and locations, times and observations, each organization’s records, prior coordination and the issue requiring a decision.

lessons.title: Plan authorized spectrum use for training
lessons.summary: Prepare a training requirement that a spectrum authority can review for coexistence and compliance.
objectives: Identify policy, range and power questions for training
Explain the purpose of validating a frequency request early
Distinguish technical compatibility from operating authorization

sections.heading: Define the service and approval boundaries
sections.text: Training uses the same shared spectrum as other local services. The manual directs planners to consider national and international rules and relevant government policy. Jurisdiction and location determine the authority involved in frequency approval. A usable request tells that authority what service is needed, the equipment involved, the intended area and dates, and the contact for changes.

sections.heading: Describe a proportionate requirement
sections.text: Range and power influence both the coverage a team needs and the chance of interference for other users. The manual calls for the minimum power needed to meet the service, within the authorization. A larger area or a different device can change the constraints. Coordinate the requirement through the relevant spectrum manager and track whether an assignment has been approved and communicated.

sections.heading: A county exercise example
sections.text: A county invites a university team to demonstrate field telemetry at a training site. The university describes its devices, planned period and coverage need to the exercise organizers. The organizers check who coordinates spectrum access there and how neighboring services are protected. If the demonstration moves, they confirm that existing conditions still apply or request a revision before relying on the original approval.

questions.prompt: Why begin a frequency request before training starts?
questions.answer: The responsible authority needs time to review conditions, coordinate with others and communicate the authorization.

questions.prompt: What does the minimum required power principle address?
questions.answer: Support the authorized service while limiting unnecessary emissions and interference risk.

questions.prompt: An approved demonstration moves to a different site. What should the organizer verify?
questions.answer: Whether the approval covers the new location and whether changes need to be coordinated with the responsible authority.

lessons.title: Spectrum inputs to the common picture and planning decisions
lessons.summary: Follow how Army staff use shared information to plan, compare options and record approved changes.
objectives: Explain the purpose of the common operational picture
Identify where spectrum inputs enter the Army planning process
Recognize when observations require a revised estimate or plan

sections.heading: Keep a shared picture
sections.text: A common operational picture gives participating commands a common view of relevant information. Spectrum staff contributes what is known about resource use, operating conditions and interference. A useful display identifies when information was collected and whether it describes an observation, a model or a planned activity. Each comes with a different kind of uncertainty.

sections.heading: Use the picture to support choices
sections.text: The Army military decision-making process begins by understanding the task and situation. Spectrum planners assess requirements and resources during mission analysis. They use the results to develop, analyze and compare options, then provide spectrum-related inputs to the plan or order. This manual identifies Annex H, Signal, as a recipient of key staff inputs. Reassessment is necessary when new observations change a material assumption.

sections.heading: A shared inspection drill
sections.text: An inspection team is choosing between two sites. Its map shows past coverage at one site and an unverified estimate at the other. A shared planning display can show both with their source and confidence. The reviewer can then ask which critical tasks rely on the estimated coverage and compare the options on the same basis. After approval, the team shares the selected arrangements and updates affected staff.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a common operational picture?
questions.answer: Give participants a shared view that supports situational awareness and collaborative planning.

questions.prompt: Which annex does ATP 6-02.70 identify for spectrum staff inputs?
questions.answer: Annex H, Signal, of the Army plan or order.

questions.prompt: One location is covered by an estimate and another has recent measurements. How should the planner present them?
questions.answer: Mark the evidence type, collection dates, assumptions and confidence so the options can be compared appropriately.

lessons.title: Spectrum dependencies across Army functions
lessons.summary: Connect the spectrum manager’s work to service continuity, safety and the functions using spectrum-dependent devices.
objectives: Identify spectrum dependencies for all six Army warfighting functions
Explain how spectrum management contributes to protection and sustainment
Recognize distinct types of electromagnetic environment hazards

sections.heading: A shared dependency across functions
sections.text: ATP 6-02.70 applies spectrum management to command and control, movement and maneuver, intelligence, fires, sustainment and protection. Communications support coordination and reporting. Movement can change which services remain available. Intelligence and fires depend on spectrum-enabled sensing, positioning or links. Sustainment needs reliable communications and tracking throughout an activity. Protection includes coexistence, interference mitigation and management of electromagnetic hazards.

sections.heading: Look for consequences at the service level
sections.text: A frequency conflict matters because it degrades a function people rely on. A logistics radio outage can delay supplies and leave coordinators with incomplete information. An electromagnetic disturbance may impair equipment performance. Radiation exposure concerns need the appropriate safety oversight. Chapter 3 also discusses electromagnetic pulses and natural effects as categories to understand when evaluating resilience and hazards.

sections.heading: A multi-service exercise example
sections.text: At a disaster response drill, one telemetry feed supports road access checks, supply deliveries and the central coordination desk. The exercise team can trace what information flows over the link and who depends on it. Before the drill, the manager confirms that the intended use fits the coordination plan. During review, the team records which functions saw degraded service and whether equipment, surroundings or uncoordinated use offer an explanation.

questions.prompt: How does spectrum management support sustainment?
questions.answer: It coordinates sufficient and compatible access for logistics systems and communications for the required period.

questions.prompt: How can spectrum management support protection?
questions.answer: By coordinating use, reducing harmful interference and identifying electromagnetic conditions that need safety or resilience review.

questions.prompt: A shared telemetry feed fails during a drill. How should the review identify impact?
questions.answer: List each dependent function, what information was lost and the observed service or safety consequence.

lessons.title: Wavelength, unwanted products and propagation
lessons.summary: Connect basic radio physics to how equipment can coexist and why an unwanted signal may appear.
objectives: Relate frequency and wavelength
Distinguish harmonics from intermodulation products
Explain how a path influences received energy

sections.heading: Frequency and wavelength
sections.text: Frequency counts oscillations per second and is measured in hertz. Wavelength is the distance occupied by one cycle. For waves traveling at the same speed, increasing frequency shortens wavelength. Amplitude describes the size of a wave’s variation from its resting value. These quantities help describe radio waves, antenna response and interaction with physical objects.

sections.heading: Why new frequencies can appear
sections.text: A harmonic occurs at an integer multiple of a fundamental frequency. Intermodulation can occur when multiple signals interact in a nonlinear component and create new frequency components related to the inputs. A receiver can be affected when sufficient unwanted energy falls within its passband. The observed component and its source must be checked before concluding which mechanism explains it.

sections.heading: A passive laboratory observation
sections.text: Two receivers observe the same demonstration source from different rooms. One sees a weaker signal and a fluctuating reading. The wall and reflected paths can affect the energy each receiver receives. A lab record should describe the geometry and conditions under which each measurement was taken. Separate that path question from the possibility of an unwanted frequency component in the equipment. The two effects may require different evidence.

questions.prompt: What happens to wavelength when frequency doubles at the same wave speed?
questions.answer: The wavelength halves.

questions.prompt: How does a harmonic differ from an intermodulation product?
questions.answer: A harmonic is a multiple of one fundamental frequency. An intermodulation product results from nonlinear interaction of multiple signals.

questions.prompt: Two rooms receive different signal levels from the same unchanged demonstration source. What physical explanation is worth checking?
questions.answer: Obstruction and reflections can change the energy arriving at the receivers, so compare the paths and surroundings.
