lessons.title: What compatibility means for spectrum records
lessons.summary: Interpret the distinction between what a planning tool does and the records it can exchange with another tool.
objectives: Distinguish tool capability from compatibility
Recognize why exchange formats need shared meanings and units
Check a harmless sample record for loss during transfer
Identify which part of a shared record needs clarification when exchanged data parses correctly but has different meanings.

sections.heading: Functions and exchanges
sections.text: Appendix B treats compatibility and capability as separate comparisons. A capability is a function such as displaying measurements, storing approvals or producing a report. Compatibility concerns the ability to exchange or reuse information between tools. Two tools may perform similar work while using different record formats. They can also exchange certain records while supporting very different analyses.

sections.heading: Check meaning as well as format
sections.text: The appendix describes several structured and tabular exchange formats. A successful import confirms that the destination can read the record’s structure. A useful test also checks meanings, units, locations, time zones, permission markers and the treatment of missing values. These details can change the interpretation of the record even when every row is accepted. Use a sample representative of the information the partners actually need to exchange.

sections.heading: A sample inventory transfer
sections.text: A team shares a small fictional equipment inventory with an exercise partner. The partner’s tool accepts the file but displays local timestamps in UTC. The team compares a known record before and after export and checks how each tool represents the time. It records the field definition and conversion expectation so all participants can interpret the same information when they assemble the common planning picture.

sections.heading: Carry uncertainty through the exchange
sections.text: A tool can accept a record and still change what downstream users believe. For example, a local team leaves a field blank to mean ‘the value is unknown.’ The receiving tool displays a blank as zero. Both tools may support the same exchange format, yet the result could be mistaken for a measured zero. In a sample exchange, include known, unknown and unavailable values. Verify their meanings with both users, and record which fields or conversions must be agreed before the exchange supports planning.

questions.prompt: What does a capability table describe?
questions.answer: Which functions each tool supports, such as analysis, presentation or reporting.

questions.prompt: What does a compatibility table help determine?
questions.answer: Which tools or formats can exchange usable information with each other.

questions.prompt: An equipment CSV loads, and two tools now disagree on when a test occurred. What should be checked?
questions.answer: Compare a known record across the two tools and verify timezone, field meaning and any conversion in the import.

questions.prompt: An inventory import accepts every entry but changes an unknown measurement to zero. What does the import establish, and what must be corrected before relying on the records?
questions.answer: The destination can read the file structure. It has changed the meaning of the unknown measurement. Agree on a representation for unknown values and verify a representative sample before treating the data as equivalent.

lessons.title: From requirements to maintained spectrum records
lessons.summary: Trace why spectrum planning continues through authorization, communication, observation and interference reporting.
objectives: Describe how policy, requirements, resources and assignments relate
Explain why life-cycle activities sometimes overlap
Distinguish a reported symptom from a confirmed cause
Distinguish a requirement in the spectrum manager’s working summary, coordination guidance in the plan, and a recorded assignment.

sections.heading: The life cycle begins with requirements and authority
sections.text: Appendix C describes twelve spectrum-management activities. The early activities establish guidance, gather and summarize requirements, and characterize the environment. These records help the staff request resources and develop a spectrum management plan. Activities can overlap and inform each other. A requirement discovered late can prompt a revision to earlier assumptions or coordination.

sections.heading: Maintain the coordination record
sections.text: An assignment and the associated operating guidance give users the information they need about approved access. The staff updates protection and coexistence records as conditions change. When interference appears, the record should include what the user observed, the affected service and what remains uncertain. Resolution addresses the problem. Reporting preserves evidence and communicates unresolved issues to the responsible organization. A history of prior reports can help staff recognize recurrence.

sections.heading: A community exercise
sections.text: An exercise organizer gathers equipment and scheduling needs from public works, event staff and a volunteer radio group. Midway through planning, one team asks to bring a new sensor. The organizer updates the inventory, coordinates the new requirement, and records the resulting decision. After the exercise, a brief interference report distinguishes observations from possible causes. The information carries forward into the planning record for the next event.

sections.heading: Read the records in order of what they establish
sections.text: Paragraph C-12 describes the requirements summary as the spectrum manager’s compilation for defining needs and informing later decisions. Paragraphs C-18 and C-19 describe the spectrum management plan as guidance for how participating groups coordinate, exchange information, and report problems. Paragraph C-20 describes making assignments as implementing that plan. When a new requirement appears, record it as a need, check whether it changes the plan’s coordination arrangements, and look for the responsible authority’s assignment before treating access as established.

sections.heading: A late addition to an exercise
sections.text: A community exercise keeps an inventory of teams that need a shared communications service. An accessibility team adds a request after the plans are distributed. Its entry establishes the need. The plan tells organizers how they coordinate late changes. The authorized arrangement establishes what access the team actually receives. If the exercise director asks whether the team can rely on the service, a screenshot of the inventory answers only the first question.

questions.prompt: Must all life-cycle activities occur in the order listed?
questions.answer: No. Some occur simultaneously and others depend on prior work.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between interference resolution and reporting?
questions.answer: Resolution seeks to address the problem. Reporting documents and communicates observations, effects and unresolved issues.

questions.prompt: A group adds an unlisted device after approvals were recorded. Which records may need revision?
questions.answer: The equipment and requirements inventory, relevant coordination and authorization records, and the instructions issued to affected users.

questions.prompt: An accessibility team is listed in the requirements summary and appears in the plan’s coordination section. Its assignment record is still pending. What can a planner tell the team?
questions.answer: The need and the coordination process are recorded. Actual access is still pending. The planner should keep that contingency visible and confirm the assignment with the responsible authority before telling the team to rely on it.

lessons.title: Write a coordination time every participant can interpret
lessons.summary: Use the manual’s 24-hour format and UTC designator to remove ambiguity in shared schedules.
objectives: Read 24-hour times and the Z designator
Interpret a date-time group
Account for the date boundary when converting local times

sections.heading: Use a shared reference
sections.text: A clock time alone is ambiguous across jurisdictions. ATP 6-02.70 describes the 24-hour clock and the use of Coordinated Universal Time as a shared reference. The Z suffix identifies UTC, spoken as Zulu in the manual. Local time can be useful when communicating with people at a site. For a schedule shared across sites, include the offset or UTC equivalent so everyone can identify the same interval.

sections.heading: Read the date and time together
sections.text: In the date-time group format, the day is followed by four digits for hours and minutes, then a time zone letter, month abbreviation and year. For example, 091615ZJUN25 means 16:15 UTC on 9 June 2025. A conversion between local time and UTC can shift the calendar day. The local offset can also depend on the date because of daylight saving or local time rules.

sections.heading: Conversion example
sections.text: A test lab in a time zone at UTC−04:00 schedules an exercise call for 22:30 local time on 9 July 2025. Adding four hours gives 02:30 UTC on 10 July, written as 100230ZJUL25. Updating the date as well as the hour ensures that a receiving team checks in on the same day and time.

questions.prompt: What does Z mean in a date-time group?
questions.answer: Coordinated Universal Time, also called Zulu.

questions.prompt: Read 030915ZSEP25.
questions.answer: 09:15 UTC on 3 September 2025.

questions.prompt: A lab uses UTC+02:00 and schedules a check for 00:15 local on 12 May 2025. What is the UTC date-time group?
questions.answer: 112215ZMAY25. Subtracting two hours moves the check to 22:15 UTC on 11 May.

lessons.title: Joint task force spectrum coordination and civil support
lessons.summary: Understand where standing frequency management and mission-specific integration meet.
objectives: Distinguish the joint frequency management office and JEMSOC in Appendix E
Identify the kinds of inputs exchanged with joint spectrum staffs
Explain why domestic response requires coordination with civil authorities

sections.heading: Standing expertise and joint integration
sections.text: Appendix E describes the joint frequency management office as a permanent combatant command organization that supports frequency management, spectrum coordination, interference resolution and host-nation relationships. The joint electromagnetic spectrum operations cell combines requirements and inputs for joint planning and coordination. In the joint task force described here, the cell supports the specific task force and draws on offices and specialists with ongoing responsibilities.

sections.heading: Understand the exchange
sections.text: The appendix traces inputs such as requests, authorization information and reports, and outputs such as coordination guidance and assignments. The applicable structure depends on the organizations involved. In domestic support, responders must account for civil authority relationships and responsible federal, state, tribal and local organizations. Interoperability includes the ability to share plans and updates as well as the ability to exchange a message.

sections.heading: A fictional emergency communications drill
sections.text: A state team joins federal and municipal responders. Each team can identify the service it needs, the resources already available to it, and the people who can approve changes. The joint coordination group can reconcile requirements and flag permissions that still need confirmation. Before the drill begins the participating groups compare their shared record of responsibilities and the process for reporting a service interruption.

questions.prompt: Which Appendix E organization is a standing part of a combatant command?
questions.answer: The joint frequency management office.

questions.prompt: What is a coordination responsibility of the JEMSOC?
questions.answer: Integrate participating components’ spectrum requirements, plans and updates across the joint effort.

questions.prompt: A municipal agency joins a domestic drill after the plan is approved. What should the coordinating staff confirm?
questions.answer: Its service needs, who authorizes its spectrum use, what information it can share and how changes or disruptions will be communicated.

lessons.title: The aircraft and the system
lessons.summary: Define what belongs to a UAS and explain how a shared operating environment complicates interpretation.
objectives: Distinguish the aircraft from the full system.
Explain the difference between a group and an aircraft type.
Separate a sighting from an assessment of intent.

sections.heading: System boundary
sections.text: The aircraft is the airborne part of an unmanned aircraft system. The system includes the people, supporting equipment, and networks that enable operation, as well as elements on the aircraft such as a payload or navigation module. Draw the boundary wide enough to account for the mission. An aircraft visible to an observer may be only one component of the activity the observer is trying to understand.

sections.heading: Two ways to describe the aircraft
sections.text: A group is a classification based on physical and flight characteristics. A type describes the aircraft's design, such as fixed-wing, rotary-wing, or hybrid. These answer different questions. The group organizes aircraft using common criteria, while the type helps explain how the airframe flies. Neither classification alone establishes who operates the aircraft, why it is flying, or whether it is authorized.

sections.heading: A shared environment
sections.text: The operational environment includes friendly and neutral activity as well as threats. Legitimate aircraft and hazardous or unauthorized activity can be present in the same airspace. A safety team can record an observation and report what remains unknown, including identity, authorization, and purpose. This preserves information for the people responsible for identification and avoids carrying a guess forward as an established fact.

questions.prompt: What else belongs in the system boundary besides the aircraft?
questions.answer: Include personnel, supporting equipment, and networks needed to operate it.

questions.prompt: Do group and type answer the same classification question?
questions.answer: Group describes a class derived from physical and flight characteristics. Type describes airframe design.

questions.prompt: A training observer sees a fixed-wing aircraft above a mixed-use area. Which assessment can the observer substantiate?
questions.answer: The observer can describe the apparent design and location. Operator, purpose, and authorization remain undetermined without additional evidence.

lessons.title: Who owns the information and the decision
lessons.summary: Trace how the commander, intelligence and operations staffs, airspace cell, and CEMA working group contribute to a shared assessment.
objectives: Identify distinct contributions of the S-2 and S-3.
Explain why the ADAM/BAE cell and CEMA working group both matter.
Use a running estimate to separate evidence, assumptions, and recommendations.

sections.heading: Intelligence and operations
sections.text: The commander directs integration across the staff and sets protection priorities. The intelligence staff develops the threat picture and communicates what collection can support. The operations staff coordinates the broader C-UAS effort with the rest of the unit's work. Their contributions meet in a running estimate, which updates the available facts, assumptions, and recommendations as the operating picture changes.

sections.heading: Airspace and spectrum
sections.text: The Air Defense Airspace Management/Brigade Aviation Element cell brings an air defense and aviation perspective to brigade coordination. The Cyber Electromagnetic Activities working group brings together contributors whose systems or responsibilities intersect in cyberspace or the spectrum. Both groups help staffs consider effects on other users, including friendly aviation and communications. Each provides a different perspective on the same incident.

sections.heading: Decision support
sections.text: A running estimate is useful when it shows where the evidence came from and which issues are unresolved. For example, an airspace record can support an identity assessment while a spectrum report can establish that interference occurred. Combining those facts can inform a commander, but causation and authority still require separate assessment. A staff recommendation should preserve those distinctions so the decision can be reviewed later.

questions.prompt: What are the roles of S-2 and S-3 in the chapter?
questions.answer: S-2 advises on intelligence and develops threat understanding. S-3 has overall planning, coordination, and supervision responsibility.

questions.prompt: What makes a running estimate useful after a new report arrives?
questions.answer: It updates the assessment and preserves distinctions among confirmed facts, assumptions, risks, and recommendations.

questions.prompt: A tabletop team sees an unidentified track and hears a radio interference report. Which perspectives should the operations staff coordinate?
questions.answer: Coordinate airspace and aviation assessment with ADAM/BAE, spectrum considerations with CEMA, and threat interpretation with intelligence staff. Keep the observations separate until evidence connects them.

lessons.title: Reading UAS threat reports
lessons.summary: Use the threat chapter to distinguish observed activity, possible roles, and statements of confidence.
objectives: Distinguish a platform's appearance from its possible role.
Separate multiple observations from proof of coordination.
Explain why corroboration can change an assessment.

sections.heading: A role is an inference
sections.text: The chapter distinguishes intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance from direct and supporting roles. A significant difference is whether the aircraft is used to collect information, plays a part in another activity, or produces an effect itself. An observer usually sees a subset of that activity. A claim about intent needs contextual evidence, including whether reported tracks are linked to one another or to another event.

sections.heading: Multiple observations
sections.text: A cluster of records can come from several aircraft, separate reports about the same aircraft, or observations that happen to overlap. A report of several objects may be important on its own. A stronger statement that they were operating as a coordinated group depends on corroboration. Separate the observation of multiple objects from the hypothesis of coordinated operation.

sections.heading: Reporting quality
sections.text: Preserve the observer's description, the source of the report, and any limits on confidence. An independent observation can support a claim that an aircraft was present while leaving its role unresolved. Record that difference explicitly. Once a conclusion gains support, note the new evidence that changed the assessment so a later reviewer can distinguish a revised judgment from the original report.

questions.prompt: Why can a report about an aircraft's presence support only a limited conclusion?
questions.answer: It confirms an observation under stated conditions. Purpose and operator require additional evidence.

questions.prompt: Do four messages necessarily represent four aircraft?
questions.answer: No. Reports may refer to the same aircraft or overlap in other ways. Compare their sources and records before counting separate objects.

questions.prompt: In an exercise, two independent observers report three objects together. What distinction should the analyst preserve?
questions.answer: There is corroboration for multiple objects appearing together. Whether the objects were coordinated is a separate judgment with its own evidence.

lessons.title: Protection priorities and layered defense
lessons.summary: Connect asset criticality, risk assessment, and complementary protection functions.
objectives: Explain why criticality and vulnerability describe different properties.
Describe how complementary layers improve resilience.
Identify dependencies that can limit the value of redundancy.

sections.heading: Criticality, susceptibility, and context
sections.text: A critical asset is important to the mission. Vulnerability describes the degree to which a hazard could affect an asset. Priority takes both into account and depends on the circumstances and consequences. Two assets may be equally exposed yet have different importance. A working assessment records why a protection priority was assigned and which changes could justify revisiting it.

sections.heading: Complementary roles
sections.text: The chapter treats layered defense as the combined contribution of successive protection functions. Local observation, wider-area awareness, information sharing, and measures that reduce consequences address different parts of the problem. Layering helps when their contributions complement each other and when the loss of one contribution leaves other useful paths available. The same shared dependency can limit several layers at once.

sections.heading: Dependency reasoning
sections.text: Imagine two safety displays that receive exactly the same underlying feed. Two screens give the team redundant display hardware, but they still share an upstream source. An exercise can compare response to a broken screen with response to missing observations upstream. This tests whether the design protects the function that matters, which in this example is maintaining an accurate picture of shared airspace.

questions.prompt: How is asset criticality different from vulnerability?
questions.answer: Criticality describes mission importance. Vulnerability describes susceptibility to an effect under the given conditions.

questions.prompt: Where does redundancy add the most value in the shared-display example?
questions.answer: It adds value when continuity covers the relevant failure, including the shared upstream source if that source is the concern.

questions.prompt: A simulated facility works normally after losing one display, but both screens lose their tracks when the same service fails. What has the test demonstrated?
questions.answer: The design tolerates failure of a display. It has a shared upstream dependency that still interrupts awareness.

lessons.title: Spectrum effects and shared-use risk
lessons.summary: Relate electromagnetic support, protection, and attack to the spectrum coordination issues that appear in C-UAS planning.
objectives: Describe the purpose of ES, EP, and EA.
Explain why induced and unintentional interference require assessment.
Identify information required to assess potential friendly effects.

sections.heading: Three related functions
sections.text: Electromagnetic support contributes observations of the electromagnetic environment to operational understanding. Electromagnetic protection preserves the ability of friendly personnel, facilities, and equipment to function despite effects in that environment. Electromagnetic attack refers to the employment of electromagnetic or directed energy for an intended effect. In planning, each provides a different perspective on how an RF-dependent activity may affect shared spectrum use.

sections.heading: Interference and attribution
sections.text: Unexpected degradation can result from an unintended change in the electromagnetic environment. A coincident activity may be relevant to the investigation, but correlation alone leaves cause unresolved. A report should distinguish the affected system, the symptoms, the operating conditions, and what changes preceded the event. Those facts allow spectrum managers and system owners to compare observations across affected services.

sections.heading: Shared effects
sections.text: Friendly aviation, communications, and other services may depend on the same environment even when their operators work in different organizations. A planning discussion should account for those dependencies, coordination responsibilities, and potential unintended effects. Test how those organizations would exchange observations during a tabletop exercise. The exercise can assess whether the right staff receives the report and whether open questions remain visible.

questions.prompt: Which EW function concerns preserving friendly use of systems in the electromagnetic environment?
questions.answer: Electromagnetic protection.

questions.prompt: What can an interference report establish without attributing its cause?
questions.answer: It can document the affected system, observed degradation, conditions, and relevant events without asserting why it happened.

questions.prompt: Two friendly services report problems after the same exercise event. What would support a defensible assessment?
questions.answer: Record evidence from both services, identify shared dependencies and changes, and coordinate review with their system owners and spectrum staff.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter 4, paras. 4-23–4-27 (pp. 26–28)

lessons.title: Passive protection and active response
lessons.summary: Understand how exposure reduction supports continuity and why identity and response are different decisions.
objectives: Explain the purpose of passive protection.
Identify what information a detection report can establish.
Distinguish identification and response authority.
Trace how a local observation becomes part of a shared air picture and identify which conclusions still require separate evidence.

sections.heading: Exposure and continuity
sections.text: Passive defense reduces the likelihood that an air threat can detect a unit or limits harm if an incident occurs. Its contribution continues even when staff are unsure that an aircraft is present. In a continuity exercise, the team can ask which protective measures preserve people and essential functions under uncertain conditions. This framing assesses resilience independently of whether anyone responds directly to an aircraft.

sections.heading: From detection to status
sections.text: A detection report says that an object or signal was observed, usually with the observer's estimate of its characteristics. Identity can draw on several forms of evidence. The chapter differentiates procedural from positive identification, both of which involve the criteria and responsibilities established for the airspace. An observation should retain enough context for the people responsible for identification to evaluate it.

sections.heading: Response responsibility
sections.text: Active defense concerns action against an air threat and carries its own decisions about authority and coordination. Reliable identification supports those decisions. A report stating that an object is present, an assessment identifying it, and an authorization for a response are three distinct statements. A useful tabletop review asks participants to identify which statement was made, by whom, and with what supporting information.

sections.heading: A local report and a shared picture answer different questions
sections.text: Appendix A describes an air-picture system that combines inputs from several kinds of sensors. A sensor contributes an observation from its own coverage. The shared-picture system brings reports together for a common view. An identification assessment assigns a status using the applicable criteria, and a decision about authority belongs to the responsible organization. Each step adds something different. A shared display helps users coordinate, while an observation missing from that display may reflect delay, coverage, or a reporting gap.

sections.heading: Preserve the time and source
sections.text: In a civilian event exercise, one observer records an object at 10:12. The shared display last refreshed at 10:08, and a second observer sees nothing from a different part of the venue. Enter the timed observation as a local report with identity unresolved. Check the display’s update status and keep the second observer’s location with their report. This preserves all three pieces of evidence without treating an older picture or a different viewpoint as proof that the first report was wrong.

questions.prompt: What is the function of passive defense in this chapter?
questions.answer: Reduce the chance of detection or limit the effects of an air threat on people and essential functions.

questions.prompt: Which distinction matters between detection and identification?
questions.answer: Detection establishes an observation. Identification establishes the object's status under the relevant criteria.

questions.prompt: A tabletop observer records a confirmed sighting with unresolved identity. How should the exercise log describe it?
questions.answer: Record it as detected and leave identity undetermined. Keep any response authorization in a separate decision record.

questions.prompt: A 10:12 local sighting is absent from a shared display last updated at 10:08. A second observer in another area saw nothing. What should the exercise log say?
questions.answer: Log the timed local report with its source and identity unresolved. Record the display’s earlier refresh time and the other observer’s different coverage. Seek a current shared record or a comparable observation before claiming agreement, disagreement, or identification.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter 5, paras. 5-1–5-4 and 5-26–5-30 (pp. 41–42, 50–51); Appendix A, paras. A-24–A-27 (pp. 81–82)

lessons.title: Air warnings, identification, and control
lessons.summary: Separate a warning about the air situation from the measures that govern identification and decision authority.
objectives: Explain what an air defense warning conveys.
Distinguish theater warnings from local context.
Describe how warning, aircraft identity, and authority serve different purposes.

sections.heading: Shared air warnings
sections.text: Air defense command and control nodes distribute warnings to communicate the assessed probability of an air attack. Local warnings can provide more specific context to units in an area. One purpose of standardized language is to give recipients a shared baseline for interpreting a report. A wider-area warning can apply even when an individual unit has no confirmed sighting.

sections.heading: Aircraft identity
sections.text: Identification is a judgment about a specific object based on established criteria and the available evidence. That judgment can change as better information reaches the appropriate authority. A higher-warning posture communicates a change in risk, while a specific track retains the status its evidence supports. A situation display can show both values side by side without implying that one establishes the other.

sections.heading: Control and authority
sections.text: The chapter distinguishes weapon control status and levels of control from the warning message. They express different decisions about where management resides and what constraints apply. During a classroom exercise, keep separate records of the warning in force, the assessment of an individual track, and the authority governing a decision. This separation makes misunderstandings easier to identify when several organizations share airspace.

questions.prompt: What does an air defense warning convey?
questions.answer: The assessed probability of an air attack and related warning information for recipients.

questions.prompt: What makes a local warning useful alongside a broader warning?
questions.answer: It adds context for an individual area or organization.

questions.prompt: A training message raises the warning while the only track remains unknown. What should change in the log?
questions.answer: Update the warning. Retain the track's unknown identity and document applicable control or authority independently.

lessons.title: Sustaining proficiency as the problem changes
lessons.summary: Connect individual, crew, and collective learning with evidence from observations and training reviews.
objectives: Distinguish individual, crew, and collective learning objectives.
Turn one exercise observation into a testable learning objective.
Assess evidence of improvement at the right level.

sections.heading: Levels of training
sections.text: Individual training builds the knowledge and skills a person needs in an assigned role. Crew training develops shared performance among people working together on a system. Collective training tests how organizations combine those contributions. A unit can have skilled individuals and still encounter a coordination problem across staff functions. Keeping the levels distinct helps instructors address the issue that the exercise actually revealed.

sections.heading: A feedback cycle
sections.text: The chapter describes observations, insights, and lessons as inputs to revising training as the environment changes. Start with what happened and under which circumstances. The observation that two staff teams used different terms for the same air track suggests a shared reporting problem. The resulting training objective might be to have both teams communicate the same track status and confidence from the same evidence.

sections.heading: Evidence of improvement
sections.text: In a follow-up tabletop, give participants a different example that requires the same interpretation and coordination. The review can assess whether the reports now agree, whether an ambiguous observation is described consistently, and whether the responsible staff can explain the outcome. Testing the learning objective with new evidence helps separate improved understanding from simple recall of the previous answer.

questions.prompt: What can a collective exercise reveal that individual testing may miss?
questions.answer: It can reveal coordination problems between people, crews, or staff organizations even when each performs its own role well.

questions.prompt: Why record the conditions that accompanied an exercise observation?
questions.answer: Conditions help establish why the result occurred and what a revised exercise should test.

questions.prompt: Everyone passes an individual quiz, but two teams still interpret the same track differently. Which training objective is most relevant?
questions.answer: A collective objective about shared interpretation and reporting, with new material used to assess whether the teams agree.

lessons.title: Reading a strategic model
lessons.summary: Relate national objectives, the competitive setting, and the operational environment in the Army's 2024 model.
objectives: Distinguish a stated objective from a prediction.
Describe why the chapter brings several instruments of national power together.
Attribute historical assessments to their source and date.

sections.heading: Objectives and perspective
sections.text: The chapter draws on Russian policy statements and the U.S. Army's interpretation to explain a strategic outlook. A published policy statement is evidence of stated priorities. An assessment about why a government made the statement or how it may behave involves interpretation. Keep those levels distinct when reading a sentence about strategic objectives, and capture the date of the documents behind it.

sections.heading: From the strategic to the operational setting
sections.text: The Army's model presents diplomacy, information, military capabilities, and economic factors as parts of a broader competitive setting. The existence of these instruments explains why the strategic overview reaches beyond military formations. Their relationship to an operational environment depends on its actors and conditions. Readers should identify which factor the text discusses before carrying a broad claim into a narrower training example.

sections.heading: Evaluating the record
sections.text: A doctrine publication makes its assumptions visible through terminology and examples. A learner can use it to understand the model it presents, then look for independent evidence before making a claim about a particular time or place. Describing a dated strategic model is useful in its own right because it shows the framework the authors used to organize later chapters.

questions.prompt: What can a quoted national policy statement establish directly?
questions.answer: It establishes what the published statement said at a documented date. Intent and later behavior require interpretation and other evidence.

questions.prompt: Why does Chapter 1 discuss economic and informational factors?
questions.answer: It situates military activity in a wider competitive setting with multiple instruments of national power.

questions.prompt: An exercise writer quotes a 2021 strategy to describe an event in 2026. How should they qualify the claim?
questions.answer: Identify the strategy and date, distinguish stated priorities from the exercise interpretation, and require contemporaneous evidence for a real-world claim.

lessons.title: Reform and institutional structure
lessons.summary: Understand the relationship among modernization, a doctrinal organization chart, and the authority that controls a force.
objectives: Describe why reform may leave more than one formation model in use.
Separate policy, service identity, and command responsibility.
Interpret an organization chart within its publication date.

sections.heading: Why organization changes
sections.text: Chapter 2 connects the military's role with reforms and developments in military thought. It describes a transition toward brigade-centered structures under New Look reforms and a later return of divisions in some cases. These examples show that an organization chart can reflect several phases of change at once. The doctrinal purpose of a formation may persist even while its name, composition, or parent organization changes.

sections.heading: Three different labels
sections.text: A service label tells the reader where an organization belongs institutionally. A command relationship tells who directs activity in a specified context. An equipment modernization initiative describes an intended change in capability over time. A single chart can show some of those relationships and leave others unexplained. Reading the accompanying text is necessary to understand the authority represented by an arrow or a box.

sections.heading: Working with dated examples
sections.text: Choose a concrete claim about the source before interpreting an example. A training chart can show that the edition used a formation of a particular type to represent a role. A claim that an identified formation has the same composition today requires a separate record. This distinction is especially useful in a chapter that documents modernization, reorganization, and joint support arrangements.

questions.prompt: Why can brigade and division models appear in the same account?
questions.answer: The chapter describes reforms and later changes that produced different models in different contexts.

questions.prompt: What does a service label establish in an organization chart?
questions.answer: It establishes institutional affiliation. The specific command or support arrangement requires context.

questions.prompt: Two editions put a similarly named formation under different headquarters. What should a learner check?
questions.answer: Check the dates, meaning of each chart's relationships, and whether the charts show standing or particular command arrangements.

lessons.title: Standing forces and task organization
lessons.summary: Interpret the relationship between a standing formation, a subordinate element, and assigned support.
objectives: Explain the source's distinction between units and subunits.
Distinguish assignment for a purpose from standing organization.
Read formation examples without projecting their composition onto every unit.

sections.heading: The publication's vocabulary
sections.text: The chapter uses SV for the Russian ground forces. In its terminology, a division, regiment, or brigade is a unit able to sustain action, while a battalion, tactical group, or subordinate detachment is a subunit that draws on support. This usage has a concrete implication for reading the examples. A named subunit may appear as the focus of a diagram while still relying on functions outside the diagram's boundary.

sections.heading: Support and ownership
sections.text: Some supporting functions belong permanently to a formation. Others can be allocated for a particular purpose under a specified command or support relationship. Compare the standing chart with the text that introduces a task-organized example. Ask where the element comes from, who provides its resources, and which headquarters is responsible for coordinating its contribution at the point described.

sections.heading: Interpretation of examples
sections.text: The chapter uses motorized rifle, tank, and other structures to illustrate the composition of ground forces. Such examples are useful as a shared vocabulary for recognizing distinct roles. Actual composition depends on time, place, organization, and the scope of the source. A study note that labels a chart as doctrinal or notional preserves a distinction the reader needs when comparing it with reports or newer editions.

questions.prompt: Which of these does the chapter call a subunit, a brigade or a battalion?
questions.answer: A battalion is a subunit in the chapter's terminology.

questions.prompt: How does temporary support differ from standing organization?
questions.answer: Temporary support assigns a contribution for a defined purpose. Standing organization describes the formation's enduring structure.

questions.prompt: A classroom diagram shows a specialist element supporting a battalion. What claim about ownership can you make?
questions.answer: The diagram shows the support relationship for that example. Permanent ownership requires the standing organizational evidence.

lessons.title: Collection, assessment, and security
lessons.summary: Connect the Russian model's reconnaissance functions to decision support and distinguish their purpose from security functions.
objectives: Distinguish collection, assessment, and dissemination.
Explain why reconnaissance and security overlap in practice.
Evaluate the independence of two source reports.

sections.heading: From collection to interpretation
sections.text: The chapter treats reconnaissance and security as continuing activities. Reconnaissance provides information about circumstances that may affect a decision. A collector's report is one input. The staff still needs to interpret how the observation bears on a question, compare it with other available sources, and communicate both the assessment and its limits to the people who will use it.

sections.heading: Related purposes
sections.text: Security supports the ability of a force to act with adequate awareness and protection. Reconnaissance can contribute to security through earlier understanding, while security functions can protect the people or systems that collect and communicate information. The same organization or technology can appear in both discussions because its contribution depends on the purpose, task, and recipient described in that example.

sections.heading: Evidence can share an origin
sections.text: The source describes a mix of manned and unmanned collection and digital distribution of information. A second report is valuable evidence when it brings a genuinely separate observation. Several staff displays can repeat information from one original source. A reviewer should trace the origin and transformation of each report before treating agreement between the displays as corroboration. The identity of the forwarding staff is distinct from the identity of the observer.

questions.prompt: What does dissemination add after an observation is made?
questions.answer: It gets the information or assessment to the people who can use it, with context and uncertainty preserved.

questions.prompt: How can reconnaissance support security?
questions.answer: It can improve awareness of changes and emerging risks, giving the supported staff better grounds for decisions.

questions.prompt: Two reports carry the same observation and both cite one source. How much corroboration did the second report add?
questions.answer: It confirms the information circulated. It adds no independent observation of the underlying event.

lessons.title: Air defense as a network
lessons.summary: Read tactical and strategic air defense relationships through the lens of sensing, communication, and decision ownership.
objectives: Distinguish tactical ground-force and aerospace responsibilities in the edition's model.
Explain how integrated awareness depends on communication.
Separate a local observation from a shared air picture.

sections.heading: Air defense across echelons
sections.text: The model describes a layered air defense network with related strategic, operational, and tactical responsibilities. Strategic air defense generally belongs to the aerospace branch in this presentation. Ground force organizations provide much of the tactical contribution. Some organizations connect levels. A diagram that combines those contributions should be read as a relationship among echelons and functions rather than a single service chart.

sections.heading: What integration adds
sections.text: The chapter brings sensing, tracking, communication, and control together in a common picture. A local sensor can produce an observation. Sharing the observation with another organization lets that organization compare it with its own information and maintain a broader picture. This relationship depends on the availability and compatibility of the systems and on staff assigning meaning consistently to the data. It also gives the wider organization a way to recognize duplicate local reports.

sections.heading: Reasoning across a handoff
sections.text: In a classroom network diagram, show which organization owns a sensor, where an observation is sent, and which authority interprets the information. Those are three separate relationships. A communication interruption may affect the shared picture while local observation remains available. The example tests whether the model is understood, regardless of the hardware exemplar used by the manual.

questions.prompt: How can one service's contribution cross an echelon boundary?
questions.answer: Its sensing, airspace, or other support can contribute to a shared picture or protection function used by another command.

questions.prompt: Which functions make a local observation available as part of an integrated picture?
questions.answer: Communication, consistent interpretation, and command-and-control processes connect local observations with the wider picture.

questions.prompt: A training network loses the ability to share local tracks, but the local sensor remains available. What still works?
questions.answer: Local observation still works. Other organizations lose that stream of evidence for the shared picture.

lessons.title: Radio-electromagnetic battle across functions
lessons.summary: Read the four REB categories and see why the manual discusses them across reconnaissance and strike chapters.
objectives: Identify the four categories the edition uses for REB.
Distinguish information support, protection, and technical control by purpose.
Explain why terminology needs a source-specific definition.

sections.heading: Where REB appears
sections.text: The Army's rendering of Russian doctrine uses radio-electromagnetic battle, or REB, across several functions. It identifies electromagnetic attack, electromagnetic protection, comprehensive technical control, and radio-electromagnetic information support measures. Chapter 4 focuses on functions supporting reconnaissance and security. Chapter 5 places attack in its discussion of strike. Appendix F collects equipment examples associated with tactical capabilities.

sections.heading: Compare purposes
sections.text: Information support contributes knowledge of the electromagnetic environment and supports other functions. Protection contributes to continued functioning of friendly systems. Comprehensive technical control concerns how friendly use is managed and monitored, including compatibility. Attack is the category associated with deliberate effects on an opponent. These role descriptions help distinguish the categories independently of the hardware associated with each one.

sections.heading: Translation and interoperability
sections.text: Different doctrine publications can use similar terms with different category boundaries. When comparing the Russian model in this ATP with another joint or Army publication, read both definitions and record the purpose of each category before setting up equivalences. Record the role of technical control explicitly: it concerns the compatibility and management of friendly use in this account. Other doctrine may place comparable responsibilities in several places in its taxonomy.

questions.prompt: Which four REB categories appear in the edition?
questions.answer: Electromagnetic attack, electromagnetic protection, comprehensive technical control, and radio-electromagnetic information support measures.

questions.prompt: Why does the text discuss REB in both Chapters 4 and 5?
questions.answer: The chapters focus on different roles. Chapter 4 addresses reconnaissance and security support, and Chapter 5 covers REB as part of strike.

questions.prompt: A comparison table equates comprehensive technical control with every U.S. EW protection activity. What should a reviewer improve?
questions.answer: Compare the source definitions by purpose and describe the overlap. Keep the distinct category boundaries visible.

lessons.title: Strike in the combined-arms model
lessons.summary: Interpret strike as a coordinated set of roles in the Army's model of Russian doctrine.
objectives: Distinguish a functional organization from its supporting platforms.
Identify why command, information, and sustainment all appear in the chapter.
Interpret related functions without inferring fielded availability.
Explain what an equipment list and a separately cited organizational passage can each establish about a support function.

sections.heading: More than an equipment grouping
sections.text: The strike chapter explains how the doctrinal model brings together information, senior decisions, and capabilities contributed by several organizations. The chapter discusses artillery, aerospace support, electromagnetic warfare, and additional means. A sketch of these relationships makes clear why a catalog of platforms describes only one part of the model. The broader function also depends on organizations collecting information, maintaining coordination, and providing support.

sections.heading: Different sources of support
sections.text: An organization may have its own capability or receive support from a higher headquarters or another service. In the model, the grouping depends on the scope and echelon of the example. A source statement that one capability can contribute should be recorded as a relationship in the model. Actual availability, readiness, and assignment in a specific event are additional factual questions.

sections.heading: Read the schematic
sections.text: Begin with the labels and the specific responsibilities documented in the text. A connection can represent reporting, direction, or support, and those relationships have different implications. Before comparing Russian material with another doctrine, write a short description of what each source says the function accomplishes. This allows comparison even when the two publications use different names for its component organizations.

sections.heading: Use an inventory and an organization passage together
sections.text: Appendix E inventories equipment in one support category. The discussion starting on page 5-26 supplies the organizational context that an inventory alone lacks. When annotating the dated model, attach each claim to the passage that can support it. An inventory can establish that the manual lists an item under a particular function. An organizational passage can establish how the model depicts that function in relation to a supported formation. A real assignment or current availability would need its own evidence.

questions.prompt: What aspect of a functional organization does an equipment catalog establish?
questions.answer: It identifies example means. Information flow, command relationships, and sustainment require other evidence.

questions.prompt: Why is command-and-control included in a chapter that also describes equipment?
questions.answer: Separate organizations have to share information and coordinate their contributions within the model.

questions.prompt: A diagram shows a specialist function supporting a formation. Can an analyst use this alone to confirm its present assignment?
questions.answer: The diagram establishes how the model represents support. A present assignment requires current verification.

questions.prompt: A student uses an equipment table to label a support function as permanently assigned to every formation in a training model. How should the annotation change?
questions.answer: Use the table to identify the listed equipment category. Read the organizational passage for what the model says about the support relationship, and qualify the claim to the formation and edition described. The table alone does not establish permanent assignment.

lessons.title: Comparing defensive and offensive purposes
lessons.summary: Compare the opening definitions in the paired chapters and relate common enabling functions to different doctrinal purposes.
objectives: Contrast the purposes identified in the two chapter openings.
Explain what stability and activeness describe in the defense model.
Identify common functions across different purposes.

sections.heading: What a chapter opening tells you
sections.text: The defense opening identifies purposes that include preserving important areas and creating favorable conditions for further action. It describes defense as requiring stability and activeness. Stability concerns the capacity to continue under pressure. Activeness reflects the source's emphasis on initiative even in a defensive posture. This strategic-level reading gives learners a way to interpret the chapter's vocabulary without practicing any described maneuvers.

sections.heading: Common functions, different objectives
sections.text: The offense chapter presents offensive action within a combined-arms framework. Both chapters rely on reconnaissance, command and control, protection, and sustainment. Their objectives and the responsibilities given to contributing organizations differ. The presence of one supporting function, such as air defense, is therefore insufficient evidence to determine which overall purpose a source describes. Examine the stated objective and the scope of the account.

sections.heading: Use chapter context in comparisons
sections.text: A training question can ask which description best fits the purpose in a passage, while keeping the answer grounded in what the passage states. Where a passage contains only an equipment label or the name of a formation, there may be too little information. Identifying that gap is a stronger reading outcome than assigning an operation type on the basis of a familiar term.

questions.prompt: Which two characteristics does Chapter 6 emphasize in its defense requirements?
questions.answer: Stability and activeness.

questions.prompt: Why do both chapters discuss common enabling functions?
questions.answer: Both depend on awareness, coordination, protection, and sustainment, with their contributions shaped by the purpose of the operation.

questions.prompt: An abstract exercise lists an intelligence staff and communications support. Can you infer the overall purpose?
questions.answer: Their inclusion alone gives insufficient evidence. Use the stated purpose and context to interpret the role of each function.

lessons.title: Keeping functions available
lessons.summary: Relate materiel support, communications, and automated information exchange to the continued operation of a formation.
objectives: Differentiate materiel support from command-and-control support.
Explain what automation changes about information movement.
Distinguish an interruption in a communications path from a loss of authority.
Distinguish a specialist function, its relationship to a supported formation, and authority over the supporting organization.

sections.heading: Two different support relationships
sections.text: Materiel technical support addresses availability of resources such as equipment, maintenance, transport, and supplies. Command and communication complexes support the movement and organization of information needed for decisions. Both are enabling functions. Each has responsible organizations and depends on resources, but their outputs differ. A worksheet that names a generic support element should specify whether it provides materiel, information services, or both.

sections.heading: Automation and meaning
sections.text: The manual describes modernized systems that can pass reconnaissance information across connected elements. Automation can help distribute a report and make it available to more recipients. Interpretation still depends on what the record means, its source and confidence, and the recipient's responsibility. A connection on a systems diagram is therefore evidence of a designed information relationship, with reliability and usage subject to conditions.

sections.heading: Authority and channel
sections.text: In a classroom example, a staff can lose a reporting service while its decision-making responsibilities continue. The change affects which information reaches a decision maker. It may also create uncertainty if staff treat an empty display as proof that there was nothing to report. Reviewing the difference between the role, the available information, and the supporting channel is central to understanding the model.

sections.heading: Read the relationship behind a specialty label
sections.text: The 2024 model describes engineers as a specialist branch that contributes to the supported formation’s mobility and protection. Appendix I describes a distinct specialist organization that provides protective support. In each case, the specialty explains the kind of contribution the manual describes. The supported formation retains its wider responsibilities. Describe the contribution separately from who controls the specialists or which personnel are available.

sections.heading: Receiving support and possessing authority
sections.text: Appendix K gives a clear example of the difference. It describes tactical formations benefiting from reporting generated by specialist organizations without controlling those organizations. A note that an organization ‘supports the formation’ can mean that it creates information or provides a service the formation uses. To describe command authority, look for a separate source statement that names the decision-maker.

questions.prompt: What does an automated reporting system contribute?
questions.answer: It supports recording or distributing information among connected organizations. The record still requires interpretation.

questions.prompt: Who owns a decision if a reporting link fails?
questions.answer: The responsible authority identified by the command relationship. An interrupted path changes available information, not the authority by itself.

questions.prompt: A classroom display becomes empty when its reporting service stops. What should the observer conclude?
questions.answer: The display has lost its input. The record now contains a gap in awareness and cannot establish the absence of activity.

questions.prompt: The manual says that a specialist group supplies information used by a formation. A diagram labels that group as commanded by the formation. What does the passage support and how would you fix the diagram?
questions.answer: It supports a reporting or support relationship. Label that relationship and show command separately only when a source establishes it. The chapter or appendix should also establish whether the relationship is standing or described only in that example.

questions.prompt: An analyst groups engineering support, specialist protective support, and the supply function under a single label because all serve the same formation. What useful distinctions does the label hide?
questions.answer: The model describes different contributions: engineers support mobility and protection, the protective specialists have a distinct protective role, and materiel support provides resources for continued activity. Shared recipients do not establish identical duties or the same command relationship.

lessons.title: People’s War and informationization
lessons.summary: Understand informationization as a doctrinal development and relate it to the difference between national strategy and tactical organization.
objectives: Explain how the Army source situates informationization in doctrinal development.
Distinguish strategic objectives, a theory of conflict, and the organization of capabilities.
Read a doctrinal concept without inferring uniform implementation.

sections.heading: Doctrine in historical context
sections.text: The Army's account traces changes in People's War through the PLA's modernization, joint operations, and growing reliance on information. The term informationization refers broadly to integrating information and networked systems into how the PLA thinks about and organizes operations. Its appearance in a doctrinal concept records a priority in the model and gives readers a framework for interpreting later chapters.

sections.heading: Levels of explanation
sections.text: National strategy explains what a state seeks to achieve and which broad resources it sees as relevant. Military thought provides a theory for how capabilities contribute. Tactical organization describes specific responsibilities or formations. The chapter moves among these levels. Learning to recognize the shift helps a reader connect related ideas without treating a national priority as evidence that a particular subordinate unit has a specific capability.

sections.heading: Application to evidence
sections.text: Record which level a claim addresses and the date of the cited evidence. An official publication can describe an aspiration toward more networked coordination, while other evidence is needed to observe implementation. Two formations may be described through the same doctrinal framework even when their resources and experience differ. A dated example should remain associated with the edition that presented it.

questions.prompt: What does informationization describe in this lesson?
questions.answer: The integration of information and networked capabilities into how the PLA conceptualizes and organizes operations.

questions.prompt: How is a strategic objective different from a tactical organization?
questions.answer: The objective states what a national or military actor seeks. An organization identifies how particular functions or responsibilities are arranged.

questions.prompt: A student uses the doctrinal term to claim every formation has the same networking capability. What evidence is missing?
questions.answer: Evidence of actual implementation, specific to the formations and time of the claim.

lessons.title: Reading theater and land-force relationships
lessons.summary: Interpret the edition's national, theater, and tactical structure and distinguish command relationships from force composition.
objectives: Distinguish national, theater, and tactical levels.
Explain the dual reporting relationship depicted in the 2021 edition.
Distinguish group army, combined arms brigade, and combined arms battalion.
Read a capability appendix for a functional contribution, then check where the dated model places the supporting organization.

sections.heading: National and theater roles
sections.text: Chapter 2 distinguishes national-level direction, services, and theater commands. The 2021 Army model describes theater commands as responsible for joint operations within their remit and services as having institutional roles for their respective forces. In the edition's peacetime description, certain forces report through both a service and a theater relationship. Read the text for the purpose and context of each relationship.

sections.heading: Land-force echelons
sections.text: The group army sits above combined arms brigades and their subordinate battalions in the model. It can also contain specialized supporting formations. The source uses different brigade examples to describe variation in how the land force organizes its capabilities. A hierarchical chart can establish lines of subordination in the example, while adjacent prose explains which support relationships may cross those lines.

sections.heading: What a diagram can establish
sections.text: A learner can trace a hypothetical brigade up to a group army and identify a support organization at the same or a higher level. A complete interpretation should distinguish standing command from support assigned in the example and describe whether the relationship is stated or inferred from a diagram. Document the date so this reading remains tied to the historical model.

sections.heading: Capability, formation, and responsibility
sections.text: Appendix B discusses fire support as a capability and inventories examples. Appendix E describes engineering and protective functions that contribute to a broader formation. Use Chapter 2 to locate the named headquarters or formation before deciding how to label either contribution. ‘Engineering’ identifies a kind of work. ‘Combined arms brigade’ identifies a formation in the model. The two labels describe different things, even when the formation receives that work.

sections.heading: Scope organizational claims to the passage
sections.text: Appendix G identifies specialized organizations in more than one service or institution. A reference to a group army example does not place every specialized unit under the same authority. When comparing two entries, note the organization the source actually names, the level it describes, and what relationship is explicit. If the text names a capability but omits its assignment, leave assignment unspecified.

questions.prompt: Why might two lines connect a service unit to superior organizations in the edition's peacetime model?
questions.answer: The lines can represent service and theater relationships with different responsibilities.

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between the group army, combined arms brigade, and combined arms battalion?
questions.answer: In the source's model the group army sits above brigades, and combined arms battalions are subordinate to brigades.

questions.prompt: A group army specialist appears in a brigade example. What should a reader check before labeling that specialist organic to the brigade?
questions.answer: Check the standing organization chart and the text describing support or attachment in the example.

questions.prompt: A student sees specialist capabilities in several parts of the 2021 model and labels them all as owned by the group army. Which source checks would make the chart defensible?
questions.answer: Identify which institution and echelon each passage actually names. Use Chapter 2 and the relevant appendix to label explicit command and support relationships separately. Leave an assignment unspecified when the source describes only a capability.

questions.prompt: A source note puts ‘engineering’ and ‘combined arms brigade’ in the same column as if they identify the same kind of entity. How should the note be organized?
questions.answer: Engineering names a function and combined arms brigade names a formation. Separate the type of contribution from the named organization, then cite the appendix and Chapter 2 for the relationship the dated model actually depicts.

lessons.title: Joint contributions in the 2021 model
lessons.summary: Trace the distinction among service identity, joint contribution, and cross-echelon support.
objectives: Identify the four organizations discussed in Chapter 3.
Explain why a land-force account addresses capabilities from other services.
Recognize the date sensitivity of the chapter's Strategic Support Force description.

sections.heading: Capabilities beyond the ground force
sections.text: The joint chapter describes the PLA Air Force, Navy, Rocket Force, and the then-existing Strategic Support Force as contributors that can affect tactical land operations. It describes some air capabilities through theater relationships and others through national headquarters. The navy discussion ties longer-range maritime operations to basing, transport, and wider command networks. Each service perspective helps explain which organization can contribute to a land-force purpose and what resources it depends on.

sections.heading: A historical support model
sections.text: The edition presents the Strategic Support Force as a national-level organization bringing together space, cyber, electromagnetic warfare, intelligence support, and information functions. The grouping reflects the institutions described by the 2021 source. Preserve the attribution and year in any study notes, especially when comparing organization names or responsibilities with later material. The model remains useful for identifying the functions the authors analyzed.

sections.heading: Institution, function, and availability
sections.text: Organization, function, and actual availability are separate fields in a source comparison. The edition might associate a capability with a joint organization, identify a type of land operation it can influence, or estimate how the relationship works. Only the specific evidence supports each claim. A date-stamped diagram makes changes easier to recognize even when terms and functions continue across editions.

questions.prompt: Which joint organizations does the chapter survey?
questions.answer: The PLA Air Force, PLA Navy, PLA Rocket Force, and the Strategic Support Force as described in the 2021 edition.

questions.prompt: Why does an account of ground tactics discuss air and maritime organizations?
questions.answer: Their information and support can influence land operations while remaining outside the ground force's standing organization.

questions.prompt: A student places the 2021 Strategic Support Force structure on a chart labeled 2026. What evidence would justify that date?
questions.answer: Independent evidence for the organization and command relationships in 2026. The publication supports a 2021 model.

lessons.title: Functional groups and system warfare
lessons.summary: Read the system warfare model through functional organization, information relationships, and dependencies.
objectives: Distinguish a standing organization from a purpose-built operational system.
Explain what functional groups contribute to the model.
Recognize a dependency shared by separate groups.

sections.heading: A system as a purpose-built organization
sections.text: The Army describes the PLA concept of system warfare as an approach that sees operations as interactions among organized capabilities. An operational system is assembled for a purpose under a command. Its subordinate groups combine capabilities relevant to their assigned functions. This gives a reader two organizational views to keep in mind. A standing structure shows enduring units, while the operational system shows how contributions are assembled in an example.

sections.heading: Information relationships
sections.text: The chapter emphasizes networks as a means of connecting otherwise distinct groups. An organization chart can show authority or membership, while an information diagram shows which people or systems exchange records. Those relationships may overlap. An effective study diagram identifies what the arrow represents, such as direction, support, or information exchange, so the same line is interpreted consistently by different readers.

sections.heading: A classroom example
sections.text: In a hypothetical relief coordination exercise, a mapping group and a logistics group share one data service. Each has a distinct function. Both still depend on the service to receive updates. That example illustrates how separate groups can retain their organizational roles while sharing an important dependency. The concept can be studied through connectivity and continuity in a non-combat exercise.

questions.prompt: What makes the example operational system distinct from a standing organization?
questions.answer: It combines capabilities for a specified purpose. A standing chart describes enduring organization.

questions.prompt: What should a learner identify on each arrow in a functional diagram?
questions.answer: The relationship represented, such as reporting, authority, or support.

questions.prompt: Two classroom groups share a data service. Why does having separate groups provide limited continuity if the service fails?
questions.answer: Their roles differ but their information path is shared, so both can lose the same input.

lessons.title: Information operations and its subcategories
lessons.summary: Read the edition's information vocabulary and recognize how technical, cognitive, and organizational concerns enter one framework.
objectives: Describe how information warfare relates to information operations.
Distinguish technical continuity questions from cognitive concerns in the source.
Explain why an information incident can have more than one plausible cause.

sections.heading: The umbrella term
sections.text: The edition describes PLA information operations as activities affecting the information environment. Information warfare, also called information confrontation in the chapter, is a subset focused on direct support to military operations. The manual groups information warfare into information attack and information defense, and places electromagnetic protection within information defense. The broader information operations concept also includes psychological functions and deception. Keep these categories visible when comparing the passage with another doctrine.

sections.heading: Different questions about the same event
sections.text: A technical review asks whether communication systems move data reliably and whether a record reached its intended recipient. A review of cognition asks how people interpreted the information, including what they considered trustworthy. Organizational questions concern responsibilities and how teams share their assessments. Several categories can be relevant to one event. An observation should retain evidence for each claim and label any inference.

sections.heading: Use a benign example
sections.text: Suppose a classroom exercise produces two inconsistent transcripts of a message. The communication record may be incomplete, or two recipients may have understood the same words differently. Preserve both records and document the chain of transmission before settling on an explanation. This reasoning exercise illustrates why a useful analysis can distinguish access to information from its interpretation and the organization's judgment about it.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter relate information warfare to information operations?
questions.answer: It treats information warfare as a component of the broader information operations concept.

questions.prompt: What question separates technical continuity from interpretation?
questions.answer: Technical continuity asks whether data arrives and remains available. Interpretation asks what meaning people draw from the available information.

questions.prompt: An exercise produces two different versions of the same message. Which distinction should the review preserve?
questions.answer: Separate differences in transmission or records from differences in interpretation until evidence supports a cause.

lessons.sourceLocator: Chapter 5, paras. 5-1, 5-14, and 5-20–5-21, fig. 5-1 (pp. 5-1–5-5); Overview of PLA Psychological Warfare (p. 5-6)

lessons.title: Reconnaissance across echelons
lessons.summary: Read the edition's model of collection, security, and information exchange across higher and lower organizations.
objectives: Explain why the source treats reconnaissance at several levels.
Distinguish ownership of a collector from use of its information.
Identify a gap in a shared assessment.

sections.heading: Different echelons, different questions
sections.text: The chapter ties reconnaissance development to the informationized environment and describes capabilities above and at the combined arms brigade. Higher echelons can bring observations together across a broader area. A brigade can contribute more local context and request answers relevant to its responsibilities. A comparison should identify the question each organization is trying to answer and the scale at which the evidence was collected.

sections.heading: Ownership and use
sections.text: One organization can own a collection capability and another organization can receive the report. Passing information between them requires a common understanding of the observation and the recipient's needs. At a higher echelon, an assessment may combine many observations. The value of that assessment to a lower echelon depends on which relevant details and uncertainties survive the process of aggregation and distribution.

sections.heading: Reconnaissance and security
sections.text: Reconnaissance contributes observations and assessments to awareness. Security applies that awareness in protecting people, assets, and freedom to make decisions. A classroom vignette can present a broad assessment containing an unknown local condition. The learner should retain the broader assessment at its supported scale and state the local question as an information gap. That gap should remain visible as the assessment moves between staffs.

questions.prompt: Why might the same event be interpreted at different echelons?
questions.answer: A higher echelon may assess wider patterns, while a brigade needs detail relevant to a narrower responsibility.

questions.prompt: What information should remain visible when reports are aggregated?
questions.answer: Source, context, relevant detail, and uncertainty should remain accessible for the questions recipients need to answer.

questions.prompt: A broad classroom assessment leaves one local report unresolved. How should the receiving team represent it?
questions.answer: Keep the broader conclusion at its supported scale and record the local condition as an open information gap.
